explanations.a: While cost tracking of change implementation is important (and may link to the change control log), it is not the primary purpose. The change control log is fundamentally a governance and traceability document, not a timesheet.
explanations.b: The change control log tracks changes but does NOT replace the project plan or the baseline. The project plan and baselines are updated separately when changes are approved — the log documents the decisions that led to those updates.
explanations.c: While some project management tools may include notification features, automated email alerts are a tool feature — not the purpose of the change control log itself.
explanations.d: The CHANGE CONTROL LOG (also called the change log) is the central repository for managing all change requests across the project lifecycle. It typically records: unique change request ID; date submitted; requester name; description of the proposed change; reason/justification; priority; status (submitted, under review, approved, rejected, deferred, implemented, validated); decision maker and decision date; impact summary; implementation date. It serves three purposes: (1) TRACEABILITY — provides an auditable record of every proposed change and its outcome; (2) VISIBILITY — gives the project manager, sponsor, and stakeholders a complete view of all change activity; (3) GOVERNANCE — ensures no change is implemented without going through the proper review and approval process. It is updated at multiple points in the change control process: when a request is received, after preliminary review, after impact assessment, upon approval/rejection decision, and after implementation and validation.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Change control process — conduct a preliminary review of change requests
questions.text: A project manager receives three change requests in one week: CR-001 requests adding a new user authentication module (significant scope addition); CR-002 requests correcting a typo in a field label (trivial); CR-003 requests changing a report date format from MM/DD/YYYY to DD/MM/YYYY (affects international users). During preliminary review, what determination should the project manager make FIRST for each CR?

answers.text: For each CR, determine: whether it is within project scope; whether it is feasible; whether it requires a full impact assessment or can be handled through a simplified process; and who the appropriate decision maker is — CR-001 likely requires full impact assessment and CCB; CR-002 may be approved directly by the PM; CR-003 requires impact assessment for internationalization effects
Reject CR-001 as out of scope and approve CR-002 and CR-003 without further review — the PM has authority over all changes
Approve all three immediately — all change requests deserve equal, expedient treatment regardless of size
Forward all three to the CCB for a decision — all change requests must go to the CCB regardless of size or complexity

explanations.a: PRELIMINARY REVIEW is the triage step in change control. The project manager examines each request to determine: (1) Is it valid and complete? (Does it describe the change clearly with a business reason?); (2) Is it within the project's scope or does it represent an entirely new project? (3) What is the complexity and potential impact? (4) What level of review does it need — simplified expedited track or full formal track? (5) Who is the appropriate decision maker — PM, sponsor, CCB? For these three CRs: CR-001 (authentication module): HIGH complexity; full impact assessment required; likely CCB approval needed; may affect schedule, budget, security architecture. CR-002 (typo fix): LOW complexity; trivial effort (minutes); PM likely has authority to approve directly or it is classified as a non-change (defect correction); no impact assessment needed. CR-003 (date format): MEDIUM complexity; appears simple but affects database storage, display logic, user training, and potentially data exchange with other systems; impact assessment needed; PM or sponsor may decide.
explanations.b: The project manager generally does not have unilateral authority to approve significant scope changes like CR-001 (new authentication module). Additionally, CR-003 appears simple but has significant internationalization implications that require impact assessment.
explanations.c: Not all change requests require the same depth of review. Applying full change control process overhead to a typo correction wastes time and adds bureaucracy without value. Conversely, approving a major scope addition without analysis risks budget and schedule impacts.
explanations.d: Routing all changes to the CCB regardless of size creates bottlenecks and disproportionate overhead for trivial changes. Change control governance defines THRESHOLDS that determine when CCB involvement is required — not all changes need the full CCB process.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Change control process — conduct impact assessments on proposed changes
questions.text: A stakeholder requests adding a real-time analytics dashboard to an ERP implementation project. The project is currently in the development phase with 6 weeks remaining. When conducting an impact assessment for this change request, which areas should the project manager analyze?

answers.text: Schedule, cost, scope, quality, risk, and resource impacts — a comprehensive impact assessment covers all project constraints affected by the proposed change
Only the schedule impact — with 6 weeks remaining, whether the change fits in the timeline is the only relevant question
Only the cost impact — the project sponsor is most concerned with budget, so cost is the only dimension that requires formal analysis
Only the technical feasibility — once it is determined to be technically possible, the project team can absorb the change within existing plans

explanations.a: A comprehensive IMPACT ASSESSMENT evaluates the proposed change across ALL relevant project constraints — commonly the six constraints: SCHEDULE: How many additional work days will this require? Does it push the delivery date? COST: What are the direct costs (development hours, software licenses, infrastructure) and indirect costs (project overhead for the extended timeline)? SCOPE: What exactly is added, and does anything need to be removed or deferred to accommodate this within the budget/timeline? QUALITY: What additional testing, performance validation, or security review is required for the analytics dashboard? RISK: What new technical risks does real-time data integration introduce? What is the probability and impact of these risks? RESOURCES: Does the team have the skills to build a real-time analytics system? Are additional SMEs needed? The impact assessment output feeds the change recommendation and the decision maker's final determination.
explanations.b: Schedule is the most visible impact with 6 weeks remaining, but again, it is one dimension. Adding a real-time analytics dashboard could also require: additional licensed software (cost); reduced scope elsewhere to fit within the schedule (scope trade-off); additional QA cycles (quality); integration with live data streams that introduces new failure modes (risk); specific subject matter expertise not currently on the team (resource).
explanations.c: Cost is one dimension of impact — but a change to a project in development also affects schedule (time to develop the dashboard), scope (what is and is not in the project), quality (testing requirements for a new complex feature), risk (new defects, integration failures), and resources (who builds it). A cost-only analysis misses critical decision information.
explanations.d: Technical feasibility is one input to the impact assessment, but 'it's technically possible' does not mean the project can absorb the change within existing plans. Every feasible change still requires analysis of cost, schedule, resource, quality, and risk impacts.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Change control process — document change recommendations for decision makers
questions.text: After completing an impact assessment for a change request, the project manager prepares a recommendation for the project sponsor. The change request involves adding a mobile interface to a web-only application. The impact assessment found a 3-week schedule increase and $45,000 cost addition, but also identified a potential 20% increase in user adoption. What should the change recommendation document include?

answers.text: A summary of the proposed change, quantified impacts (schedule +3 weeks, cost +$45K), identified risks, potential benefits (20% adoption increase), available options (approve as-is, defer to Phase 2, reject), and the PM's recommendation with rationale — enabling an informed decision
A recommendation to reject the change — any change that adds cost and time should be rejected to protect the project baseline
Only the cost and schedule impacts — the decision maker needs hard numbers, not qualitative benefits analysis
Only the PM's recommendation — the sponsor does not need the supporting analysis, just the final answer

explanations.a: A well-formed CHANGE RECOMMENDATION document provides everything the decision maker needs: (1) Summary of the proposed change and business justification; (2) Quantified schedule impact: +3 weeks to delivery date; (3) Quantified cost impact: +$45,000 (broken down if possible: development, testing, infrastructure); (4) Risk analysis: new risks introduced (mobile browser compatibility, security for mobile data, testing complexity) and their likelihood/impact; (5) Benefits: projected 20% increase in user adoption — quantified if possible (what is 20% adoption increase worth in revenue or productivity?); (6) Options available: Option A: Approve full scope addition; Option B: Defer mobile interface to Phase 2 release (no impact on current project); Option C: Reject; (7) PM recommendation with rationale: 'We recommend Option B — defer to Phase 2 — because the current 3-week schedule addition risks missing the Q4 go-live date, and the mobile interface can be delivered as an enhancement within 60 days post-launch.' This gives the sponsor everything needed to decide without requiring them to do their own analysis.
explanations.b: Not all changes with cost and schedule impact should be rejected — changes that deliver strategic value exceeding their cost may be approved by increasing the project budget. The PM's role is to provide objective analysis, not to pre-decide based on a simple rule.
explanations.c: Decision makers need both quantified impacts AND the business context (benefits, risks, strategic alignment) to make an informed decision. A sponsor seeing only '$45K cost increase' without the '20% adoption increase' benefit lacks the information needed for a balanced judgment.
explanations.d: Providing only the final recommendation without supporting analysis puts the decision maker in a position where they cannot evaluate the PM's judgment, cannot make their own risk assessment, and cannot articulate the rationale for their decision to other stakeholders or governance bodies.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Change control process — determine decision makers; escalate to CCB if applicable
questions.text: A project's change control plan defines three authority levels: the project manager can approve changes up to $5,000 and 2 days schedule impact; the project sponsor can approve changes up to $25,000 and 1 week impact; the CCB handles anything exceeding those thresholds. Three change requests arrive: CR-A requires $3,000 and 1 day; CR-B requires $18,000 and 5 days; CR-C requires $60,000 and 4 weeks. Who approves each?

answers.text: CR-A: CCB; CR-B: CCB; CR-C: CCB — all changes should go to the CCB to ensure consistent governance
CR-A: Project Sponsor; CR-B: Project Sponsor; CR-C: Project Manager (they know the project best)
CR-A: Project Manager; CR-B: Project Manager (cost within $5K threshold); CR-C: Project Sponsor
CR-A: Project Manager; CR-B: Project Sponsor; CR-C: CCB — each CR is routed to the lowest authority level that has sufficient approval authority

explanations.a: Routing all changes to the CCB regardless of thresholds defeats the purpose of having tiered authority levels. Change control governance uses thresholds specifically to enable efficient handling of lower-impact changes without requiring full CCB review for every minor modification.
explanations.b: Authority is defined by the change control plan's thresholds, not by who is most familiar with the project. The PM's familiarity does not grant them authority over changes exceeding their defined thresholds.
explanations.c: CR-B's $18,000 cost exceeds the PM's $5,000 authority threshold — the PM cannot approve this. Additionally, CR-B's 5-day schedule impact exceeds the PM's 2-day authority. Option C incorrectly assigns both CR-B and CR-C to levels without sufficient authority.
explanations.d: Threshold-based change authority routing: CR-A ($3,000, 1 day): BOTH impacts are within PM authority ($5,000 max, 2-day max) → Project Manager approves. CR-B ($18,000, 5 days): Cost ($18,000) exceeds PM authority ($5,000) but is within sponsor authority ($25,000). Schedule (5 days) exceeds PM authority (2 days) but sponsor authority is 1 week = 7 days; 5 days < 7 days. BOTH impacts are within sponsor authority → Project Sponsor approves. CR-C ($60,000, 4 weeks): Cost ($60,000) exceeds both PM ($5,000) and sponsor ($25,000) authority. Schedule (4 weeks) exceeds both PM (2 days) and sponsor (1 week) authority. → Requires CCB approval. The principle: route to the LOWEST authority level with sufficient jurisdiction for BOTH dimensions (cost AND schedule). If either dimension exceeds a level's authority, escalate to the next level.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Change control process — escalate to the CCB; CCB structure and function
questions.text: The Change Control Board (CCB) is meeting to review a change request to migrate the project's database from on-premises SQL Server to a cloud-hosted PostgreSQL platform mid-project. Which individuals are MOST appropriate to include on the CCB for this decision?

answers.text: Representatives with decision authority over the change's impacts: project sponsor (budget/timeline authority), project manager (project impact knowledge), IT architecture lead (technical feasibility), security/compliance officer (cloud migration regulatory implications), and operations manager (production operations impact)
Only the project manager and sponsor — the CCB should be kept small to enable fast decisions
The entire development team — the people doing the work should make the decision about what technology to use
Only external vendors — database migration decisions should be made by database technology specialists who are neutral parties

explanations.a: The CHANGE CONTROL BOARD composition should match the nature and impact of changes it reviews. For a database platform migration mid-project, the CCB needs: PROJECT SPONSOR: holds budget authority (this change likely increases cost for cloud migration, re-coding, testing); can approve budget increase or scope trade-off; PROJECT MANAGER: owns the project plan and can quantify schedule impact; IT ARCHITECTURE LEAD: evaluates technical feasibility, PostgreSQL compatibility with existing code, migration complexity, and long-term architectural implications; SECURITY/COMPLIANCE OFFICER: cloud migration may have data residency, encryption, access control, and regulatory compliance (SOX, HIPAA, GDPR) implications; OPERATIONS MANAGER: production operations team will manage the cloud database going forward — their input on operational readiness and support model is essential. The CCB should have enough expertise to make an informed decision and enough authority to execute the decision.
explanations.b: A CCB with only the PM and sponsor may lack the technical expertise to evaluate the feasibility and risks of a database platform migration, the security officer's perspective on cloud compliance, and the operations perspective on production migration risks.
explanations.c: The development team provides valuable technical input during the impact assessment phase, but the CCB is a decision-making governance body — not a technical working group. Developers typically do not hold budget authority or organizational decision-making power for major architectural changes.
explanations.d: External vendors may provide technical input and proposals, but they should not be members of the CCB — they have a commercial interest in the decision and lack organizational authority. They can be consulted but should not vote.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Change control process — document the status of approval in the change control log; communicate change status
questions.text: The CCB meets and REJECTS a change request to add a third-party payment gateway integration. Two weeks later, a different stakeholder submits an almost identical change request, claiming they were unaware the earlier request was rejected. What change control failure does this reveal, and how should it have been prevented?

answers.text: The CCB met too infrequently — weekly CCB meetings would have caught the duplicate submission sooner
The duplicate submission is not a problem — stakeholders may submit the same change multiple times, and each submission should be evaluated independently
The project manager should have personally contacted every stakeholder after the rejection to prevent future submissions

The change control log was not updated with the rejection status and the rejection was not communicated to stakeholders — proper documentation of approval status and communication would have prevented the duplicate submission

explanations.a: CCB meeting frequency is a governance decision — weekly meetings would not prevent duplicate submissions if the rejection decision is not documented and communicated. The issue is documentation and communication, not meeting cadence.
explanations.b: Duplicate submissions waste CCB time, create governance confusion, and may produce inconsistent decisions if the second submission happens to be reviewed by a different CCB composition. Preventing duplicates through proper documentation and communication is a core change control objective.
explanations.c: Personal outreach to every stakeholder after every rejection is not scalable. The solution is systematic: update the log (accessible to all) and issue a change status communication (via email, project status report, or project portal) that reaches all relevant parties.
explanations.d: Two steps of the change control process were missing: (1) DOCUMENT APPROVAL STATUS IN THE CHANGE CONTROL LOG: after the CCB rejected the request, the log entry should have been updated to reflect: status = Rejected; decision date; CCB decision rationale; notes on what would be needed to reconsider. This creates a searchable, auditable record so any future submission can be cross-referenced. (2) COMMUNICATE CHANGE STATUS: the project manager should have communicated the rejection decision to relevant stakeholders — the requester, the project team, and any stakeholders who might be affected or interested. Proper communication would have informed the second stakeholder that a similar request was already rejected, along with the reasoning, preventing the duplicate submission and the wasted time of a second review.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Change control process — communicate change status; update the project plan after approval
questions.text: A change request to add multi-language support to the project has been approved by the CCB. The project manager must now communicate the change status and update the project plan. In what ORDER should these actions occur?

answers.text: Update the project plan first, then communicate to the team, then notify stakeholders — internal updates before external communication
Communicate only after full implementation is complete — stakeholders should not be informed of plan changes until the change is actually delivered
The order does not matter — as long as both actions happen within the same week, sequencing is irrelevant

Communicate the approval to the project team and key stakeholders first; then update the project plan (schedule, budget, scope baseline, resource assignments) to reflect the approved change; then ensure all team members are working from the updated plan

explanations.a: Updating the project plan before communicating to the team creates a window where some team members are working from the old plan and some from the new one, with no one aware of the change yet. Communication should be simultaneous with or precede plan distribution.
explanations.b: Communicating only after full implementation keeps stakeholders in the dark about approved scope changes for weeks or months. Stakeholders need timely change communication to adjust their own plans, manage expectations, and coordinate downstream activities.
explanations.c: Sequencing matters because: if the plan is updated before communication, team members may receive tasks for scope they don't know is approved; if stakeholders are informed before the plan is updated, they may ask questions the project manager cannot yet answer; uncoordinated actions create confusion and rework.
explanations.d: Post-approval change control sequence: (1) COMMUNICATE CHANGE STATUS: notify the requester (change is approved); brief the project team on what was approved and why — the team needs to know before they see plan updates; inform affected stakeholders of the change and its implications; update the change control log status to 'Approved'. (2) UPDATE THE PROJECT PLAN: revise the schedule to reflect additional time for multi-language development, testing, and localization; update the budget baseline to include the approved additional cost; update the scope statement/WBS to include multi-language as a deliverable; update resource assignments if new skills (translators, localization engineers) are needed; update the risk register if new risks were identified. (3) ENSURE WORKING FROM UPDATED PLAN: distribute the updated plan to the team; confirm everyone is working from the new baseline, not the old one. This sequence ensures the team has context for plan changes before the changes hit their work queues.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Change control process — update the project plan; implement changes; validate change implementation
questions.text: A change request to redesign the user interface has been approved and the project plan has been updated. The development team has completed the redesign. Which step in the change control process occurs NEXT, and what does it involve?

answers.text: Validate the change implementation — confirm that the redesigned UI meets the acceptance criteria defined in the change request, functions correctly, and has not caused unintended effects in other parts of the system
Archive the change request — once the implementation is complete, the change log entry is closed and no further action is required
Submit a new change request — every completed change requires a follow-up change request to confirm the work is done
Communicate change deployment — immediately inform all end users that the new UI is live before any testing is performed

explanations.a: VALIDATE CHANGE IMPLEMENTATION is the penultimate step in the change control process. Validation involves: Acceptance testing: verify the redesigned UI meets the acceptance criteria specified in the change request (functionality, performance, accessibility); Regression testing: ensure the UI redesign has not broken existing features that were working before the change; Stakeholder review: the requester or product owner reviews and formally accepts the implementation; Defect tracking: any issues found during validation are logged and resolved before the change is considered complete. Only after successful validation does the change control process proceed to the final step: communicate change deployment. Skipping validation risks pushing broken or incomplete implementations to production and missing defects that were introduced by the change.
explanations.b: Archiving without validation risks deploying defective or incomplete implementations. The change control process requires validation to confirm the implementation meets its intended objectives before the change can be considered complete and the change log entry closed.
explanations.c: Submitting a new change request for every completed implementation would create endless administrative cycles. Change requests are for proposed scope/plan modifications — not for confirming work completion. Work completion is tracked through project status and testing.
explanations.d: Communicating deployment to end users before validation is complete is premature. If the implementation has defects, communicating deployment would either be false (the change is not truly ready) or would expose users to a broken system. Communicate deployment AFTER validation confirms the implementation is correct and ready.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Change control process — implement changes; validate change implementation; communicate change deployment
questions.text: During implementation of an approved change (adding single sign-on integration), the development team discovers that the SSO library is incompatible with the legacy database schema and the implementation will take 3 additional weeks beyond the approved timeline. What should the project manager do?

answers.text: Initiate a new change request for the additional 3 weeks of schedule impact — the implementation discovery represents a variance from the approved change scope and timeline that must go through change control
Allow the team to take the additional 3 weeks without documentation — minor implementation discoveries during approved changes do not require change control
Instruct the team to work overtime to meet the original approved timeline — the change was approved and the team must deliver within the approved parameters
Cancel the SSO integration entirely and mark the original change as rejected retroactively

explanations.a: When a change IMPLEMENTATION reveals that the actual effort, cost, or schedule will materially exceed the approved parameters, the project manager must initiate a NEW change request for the variance. This new CR documents: the technical discovery (SSO library/legacy DB incompatibility); the additional 3-week schedule impact; options (proceed with additional time, find an alternative SSO library, defer SSO to a future phase); a recommendation. The appropriate decision maker (sponsor or CCB, depending on authority thresholds) then decides whether to authorize the additional time or choose an alternative course. This maintains governance integrity — no change implementation silently overruns its approved budget/timeline without documented authorization.
explanations.b: An additional 3 weeks of schedule impact is not a trivial implementation detail — it is a significant variance from the approved change that affects the project baseline. Change control exists precisely to handle these discovery-during-implementation situations. 'Minor implementation discoveries' without change control create undocumented schedule changes that violate project governance.
explanations.c: Instructing overtime to meet an unrealistic timeline does not address the root issue — the original impact estimate was based on incomplete information about the legacy database compatibility. Forced overtime may produce poor-quality work and team burnout without solving the technical problem.
explanations.d: Canceling an approved change retroactively and re-marking it as rejected misrepresents the project history and disrupts the stakeholder expectations set by the approved change. If the change cannot be completed as originally designed, that is a new situation requiring new decision-making — not a retroactive reversal.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Change control process — validate change implementation; communicate change deployment
questions.text: A project manager is validating the implementation of an approved change that added automated email notifications to a project management system. Testing confirms the notifications send correctly. However, a QA engineer reports that since the email module was deployed, the performance of the reporting module has degraded by 40%. What should the project manager do?

answers.text: Do NOT mark the change as validated — the performance regression is an unintended consequence of the change implementation; log the regression as a defect, investigate the root cause, and resolve it before declaring the change complete and communicating deployment
Mark the change as validated and communicate deployment immediately — the reporting performance issue is a separate project issue
Close the change as complete — the email notifications are working correctly, which was the scope of the change
Revert the change immediately — any regression caused by a change means the change must be rolled back

explanations.a: VALIDATION must confirm two things: (1) The change delivers what was intended (email notifications work ✓); (2) The change has NOT caused unintended negative effects (FAIL — 40% reporting performance degradation ✗). Because validation step 2 has failed, the change cannot be declared validated. Correct actions: Log the performance regression as a defect linked to the change; investigate the root cause (resource contention? shared database connection pool? background email processing consuming reporting resources?); fix the root cause; re-run regression tests; only after the regression is resolved and retested can the change be declared validated and deployment communicated.
explanations.b: A 40% performance degradation directly caused by the deployed change is NOT a 'separate project issue' — it is a consequence of the change that occurred during validation testing. Communicating deployment while a known regression exists would expose the production environment to a degraded reporting system.
explanations.c: Closing the change as complete when a significant regression has been identified in another system component is irresponsible. Change validation specifically includes REGRESSION TESTING to detect unintended effects — this is exactly what the QA engineer discovered. A 40% performance degradation in the reporting module is a serious unintended consequence.
explanations.d: Reversion is one option if the root cause cannot be quickly resolved, but it is not automatically required. If a targeted fix can address the performance regression without reverting the entire email module, that is preferred. The decision to revert vs. fix depends on the severity, fix timeline, and business impact — not on an automatic rollback rule.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Change control process — communicate change deployment; maintain stakeholder awareness
questions.text: An approved change (adding a new vendor portal to a procurement system) has been validated successfully. The project manager is now communicating the change deployment. Which communication approach is MOST appropriate?

answers.text: Send one brief email to the entire organization saying 'The vendor portal is now live' — keep deployment communication minimal to avoid overwhelming stakeholders
Communicate to the internal project team only — external vendors should discover the new portal by attempting to log in
Only communicate the deployment after all vendors have successfully logged in at least once to confirm they can access the portal

Tailor deployment communications by audience: notify the procurement team and system administrators with technical details (access setup, configuration); send vendors user-oriented guidance (how to register and use the portal); brief senior management with business impact summary; update the change log entry to 'Implemented'; and confirm training/support resources are available

explanations.a: A single brief email to the entire organization fails to provide relevant, actionable information to different stakeholder groups. Vendors need registration instructions; system admins need configuration guidance; senior management needs a business impact summary. One-size communication serves no one well.
explanations.b: Vendors discovering the portal by 'trying to log in' would produce confusion, support calls, and frustration. Stakeholder communication is a core component of change deployment — it ensures all affected parties know what changed, how it affects them, and what action (if any) they need to take.
explanations.c: Waiting for all vendors to successfully log in before communicating would delay the deployment announcement indefinitely — some vendors may never log in without first being told the portal exists and how to access it. Communication drives adoption; adoption cannot drive communication.
explanations.d: COMMUNICATE CHANGE DEPLOYMENT, the final step of the change control process, involves AUDIENCE-TAILORED communications: Internal project team/PMs: change log updated; confirmation the change is implemented and the sprint/task is closed. System administrators/IT: technical configuration details, access management, monitoring setup. Procurement team (internal users): new portal features, updated workflows, training resources. Vendors (external users): registration instructions, portal walkthrough, help desk contact. Senior management/sponsor: business value delivered (vendor portal reduces procurement cycle time by X days), risks mitigated. The change control log entry is updated to 'Implemented' with the deployment date. Support resources (FAQ, training, help desk awareness) should be confirmed ready before communication goes out.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Change control process — product change vs. project change
questions.text: A project is delivering a new inventory management system. Two change requests arrive: CR-1 asks for the inventory dashboard to display units in metric (kg) instead of imperial (lbs) to support international operations — this changes what the PRODUCT does. CR-2 asks for the project's testing phase to be compressed from 4 weeks to 2 weeks to meet a new corporate deadline — this changes HOW the project is managed. How should these be classified and why does the distinction matter?

answers.text: Both are project changes — all change requests affect project management and therefore are classified the same way

CR-1 is a PRODUCT change (changes the deliverable's functionality and requirements); CR-2 is a PROJECT change (changes the project management plan — specifically the schedule and quality assurance approach); the distinction matters because they route to different decision makers and carry different impact areas
CR-1 is a project change because it will require additional development time; CR-2 is a product change because the compressed timeline will affect the quality of the product delivered
The distinction between product and project change has no practical significance — both go through the same change control process identically

explanations.a: Classifying all changes as 'project changes' obscures the important distinction between changes to the thing being built (the product) and changes to how the project is managed. These have different governance implications.
explanations.b: The PRODUCT CHANGE vs. PROJECT CHANGE distinction: PRODUCT CHANGE (CR-1 — metric vs. imperial): Modifies what the deliverable does, looks like, or contains. Affects: product requirements; scope baseline (what is built); development/testing work; user documentation and training. Decision makers: typically product owner, sponsor, and/or CCB; they evaluate whether the product change aligns with business needs and requirements. Impact analysis focuses on: user impact; downstream system integrations; compliance/standards; development effort. PROJECT CHANGE (CR-2 — compressed testing): Modifies how the project is managed — the schedule, quality plan, budget, resource plan, or risk management approach. Affects: project schedule baseline; quality assurance plan (4-week testing provides different defect detection than 2-week testing); risk profile (compressed testing increases production defect risk). Decision makers: project manager (within authority), sponsor, or CCB depending on thresholds; they evaluate whether the management change is feasible and whether the risk trade-offs are acceptable. WHY THE DISTINCTION MATTERS: Different governance routes; Different impact analyses; Different risk profiles; Mixing the two leads to misrouting decisions (a product owner shouldn't decide to compress testing timelines; a technical PM shouldn't decide to change product units without business stakeholder input).
explanations.c: CR-1 affects development work but is fundamentally a product requirements change — what the product displays. The fact that it has development implications doesn't make it a project management change. CR-2 affects product quality indirectly, but it is primarily a change to the project management plan (schedule, quality approach).
explanations.d: While both change types use the same general change control framework (create request → log → review → impact assess → decide → implement → validate → communicate), the CONTENT of the impact assessment and the appropriate DECISION MAKERS differ based on whether it is a product or project change.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Change control process — manage scope creep/scope change
questions.text: A project manager is leading a 6-month software project. Over the first 3 months, the following occurred without formal change requests: the UI team added 12 extra screens 'to make it more complete'; a developer added an export-to-PDF feature because a stakeholder mentioned wanting it; the database team added audit logging 'just in case it's needed.' The project is now 3 weeks behind schedule and 15% over budget with no documented approved changes. What is happening and what corrective actions should the project manager take?

answers.text: The team is being productive by adding value proactively — the project manager should revise the timeline and budget upward to accommodate the additions

The project is experiencing scope creep; the project manager must stop unauthorized additions immediately, formally assess what was added vs. what was originally approved, submit retroactive change requests or remove the unauthorized additions, and reinforce the change control process with the team
The team should continue adding features — in Agile projects, scope additions without formal change requests are expected and acceptable
The project manager should document all additions in the project plan and present them to the sponsor as completed features to avoid stakeholder concern about the scope growth

explanations.a: Revising timelines and budgets upward to accommodate unauthorized additions without sponsor approval is itself a change control violation. The sponsor approved the original scope, budget, and timeline — expanding all three without authorization is a governance failure.
explanations.b: This is SCOPE CREEP — uncontrolled expansion of project scope without corresponding changes to schedule, budget, or resources through formal change control. Corrective actions: (1) STOP unauthorized additions immediately: communicate clearly that no features, screens, or capabilities may be added without a formal change request and approval; (2) AUDIT what was added: inventory all unauthorized additions (12 extra screens, PDF export, audit logging); assess their business value and technical completeness; estimate the schedule and budget consumed; (3) DETERMINE what to do with each unauthorized addition: Option A — submit a retroactive change request for sponsor approval to keep the addition (with documented cost/schedule impact); Option B — remove the addition and revert to the approved baseline; (4) REINFORCE change control: conduct a team meeting explaining WHY change control exists; clarify that 'adding value proactively' without authorization puts the project at risk; ensure everyone knows the change request process; (5) PRESENT to sponsor: brief the sponsor on the scope creep situation, current budget/schedule status, and the plan to get back on track.
explanations.c: Even in Agile projects, scope additions require some form of formal authorization — in Scrum, new features are added to the product backlog and prioritized by the product owner; they do not bypass governance. The premise that Agile means 'add anything without authorization' is false and dangerous.
explanations.d: Documenting unauthorized additions in the plan and presenting them as completed features without sponsor awareness conceals a governance violation. The sponsor approved a specific scope and must be informed when that scope has been materially exceeded without their knowledge or consent.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Change control process — manage scope creep; scope change management
questions.text: A project manager wants to prevent scope creep on a 9-month enterprise software project. Which combination of practices MOST effectively prevents scope creep throughout the project?

answers.text: Lock the scope document in a shared drive with read-only access — preventing stakeholders from editing the document prevents scope changes
Hold a scope review meeting at the end of the project to identify any unauthorized additions — end-of-project review catches scope creep before final delivery
Only accept scope change requests during the first month of the project — a time-limited change window prevents late scope additions

Develop a detailed scope baseline with explicit in-scope/out-of-scope statements; implement a formal change control process with documented authority levels; educate the team that any stakeholder request outside the approved scope must be directed to a change request; conduct regular scope reviews at key milestones to compare actual deliverables against the baseline

explanations.a: Read-only document access is a document control measure, not scope management. Stakeholders can still verbally request changes, and team members can still implement unauthorized additions without editing the document. Scope creep is a people and process problem, not a document access problem.
explanations.b: End-of-project scope review is far too late — unauthorized scope additions will have already consumed budget and schedule resources. By month 9, the damage of 9 months of scope creep is already done. Scope monitoring must be continuous throughout the project.
explanations.c: A time-limited 'change window' (first month only) is an extreme measure that ignores legitimate business reasons for scope changes that emerge mid-project (regulatory changes, market shifts, discovery findings). More importantly, it does not prevent unauthorized additions — it only stops formal change requests. Unauthorized additions (the actual source of scope creep) can happen at any time regardless of a formal change window.
explanations.d: Scope creep prevention is a multi-layered discipline: (1) DETAILED SCOPE BASELINE: a well-defined scope statement with explicit 'IN SCOPE' and 'OUT OF SCOPE' statements eliminates ambiguity. Stakeholders cannot argue that something is in scope if it is explicitly listed as out of scope. (2) FORMAL CHANGE CONTROL PROCESS: a documented process with authority levels ensures that proposed additions go through analysis and approval before work begins. (3) TEAM EDUCATION: every team member must know that all stakeholder requests outside the baseline must be captured as change requests — not implemented directly. This is the frontline defense against scope creep. (4) REGULAR SCOPE REVIEWS: at milestones, sprint reviews (Agile), or stage gates (Waterfall), compare actual deliverables and work in progress against the approved scope baseline. Early detection enables early correction.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Change control process — project-specific change control in Agile vs. Waterfall contexts
questions.text: A project sponsor argues: 'We're using Scrum, so we don't need a formal change control process — the product owner just adds things to the backlog.' A project manager disagrees. Which argument BEST supports the project manager's position?

answers.text: The project manager is wrong — in Scrum, the product owner has unlimited authority to add any work to the backlog without any governance review

The project manager is correct that governance is still needed, but Scrum's change mechanism is the product backlog and sprint review — the product owner formally controls what enters the backlog, serves as the CCB equivalent, and the sprint review provides the change validation step; 'formal change control' in Agile is embedded in the Scrum process itself, not eliminated
The project manager is correct that formal change control is needed because Scrum does not include any mechanism for managing scope changes
The sponsor is correct for backlog items, but a separate change control process is required for any change that costs more than $10,000

explanations.a: The product owner does not have unlimited, ungoverned authority. The product owner must justify backlog additions in terms of business value, strategic alignment, and feasibility. For major scope additions, sponsor approval, budget authorization, and resource decisions are still required — especially in organizational contexts where the Scrum team does not have unlimited funding.
explanations.b: Agile does NOT eliminate change management — it EMBEDS change management in the iterative process. In Scrum: BACKLOG AS CHANGE MECHANISM: new change requests become backlog items; the product owner evaluates feasibility and business value before adding to the backlog — this is the preliminary review and recommendation step. PRODUCT OWNER AS CHANGE AUTHORITY: the product owner has the authority to accept or reject change requests within their defined authority level (similar to a project manager's authority threshold). For changes exceeding the PO's authority (major budget increases, strategic scope shifts), escalation to sponsor/steering committee is still required — this is the CCB equivalent. SPRINT REVIEW AS VALIDATION: the sprint review validates that implemented changes meet acceptance criteria — this is the validation step. TRANSPARENCY: the backlog is visible to all stakeholders, providing the change log equivalent. The difference from Waterfall change control is that Agile change management is CONTINUOUS and LIGHTWEIGHT rather than formal and document-heavy — but the governance principles (all changes reviewed, prioritized, authorized, implemented, and validated) still apply.
explanations.c: Scrum does have a scope change mechanism: the product backlog. Saying 'Scrum has no mechanism for managing scope changes' misrepresents how Scrum works. The issue is not whether a mechanism exists but whether the mechanism provides appropriate governance.
explanations.d: A $10,000 threshold for formal change control is arbitrary. In Agile, governance thresholds are defined by the organization's project governance framework — not by a universal dollar amount.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Change control process — change control log content and management throughout project lifecycle
questions.text: A project manager is setting up the change control log for a new 12-month project. Which set of fields should the log include to support full traceability of all change requests?

answers.text: Change description and approval date only — keeping the log simple reduces administrative overhead

Change ID, date submitted, requester, description, justification, priority, current status, decision maker, decision date, schedule impact, cost impact, implementation date, and validation date — comprehensive traceability across the full change lifecycle
Only fields required by the project sponsor — the log should be customized based on stakeholder preference rather than comprehensive governance standards
Change description, team member assigned, and hours worked on the change — tracking implementation effort is the primary purpose of the change log

explanations.a: A log with only description and approval date cannot support traceability, audit, or governance. It cannot answer basic questions like: Who requested the change? What was the business justification? What was the schedule impact? Was the implementation validated? A minimal log fails its governance purpose.
explanations.b: A comprehensive CHANGE CONTROL LOG supports the full change lifecycle with these fields: INTAKE fields: Unique Change ID (for reference and tracking); Date submitted; Requester (name/role); Change description (what is being proposed); Justification/business reason; Priority (low/medium/high/critical). REVIEW fields: Preliminary review outcome; Impact assessment summary (schedule +X days, cost +$Y); Change recommendation. DECISION fields: Decision maker(s); Decision (approved/rejected/deferred); Decision date; Conditions of approval (if any). IMPLEMENTATION fields: Assigned implementer; Target implementation date; Actual implementation date. CLOSURE fields: Validation date; Validation outcome; Communication date; Final status (implemented, closed, rejected, deferred). This structure ensures that anyone (including auditors, new team members, or the project sponsor) can understand the complete history of any change at a glance.
explanations.c: While stakeholder preferences matter for format and tool selection, a governance document like the change control log must meet minimum completeness requirements regardless of sponsor preference. A sponsor who prefers a simpler log is not relieving the project of its governance obligations.
explanations.d: Hours worked is a timesheet/cost tracking field, not a change log field. The primary purpose of the change log is GOVERNANCE and TRACEABILITY — not effort tracking. Effort tracking belongs in the project schedule or resource management tools.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Change control process — all 15 steps applied in a realistic project scenario
questions.text: A project manager receives a request from the CIO to add a cybersecurity compliance module to a project that is 70% complete. Trace the CORRECT sequence of change control steps for this request, identifying what happens at each key step.

answers.text: (1) Implement immediately because the request came from the CIO → (2) Document in log → (3) Validate → (4) Communicate

(1) Create a change request and log it → (2) Preliminary review (feasibility, completeness, scope validation) → (3) Impact assessment (schedule, cost, quality, risk) → (4) Document recommendation → (5) Determine decision maker (scope and cost likely require CCB at 70% completion) → (6) CCB review and decision → (7) Log approval status → (8) Communicate decision → (9) Update project plan → (10) Implement → (11) Validate implementation → (12) Communicate deployment
(1) Reject the request — changes at 70% completion are not permitted by project management best practice → (2) Log the rejection → (3) Communicate to CIO
(1) Ask the CIO to wait until the project is complete → (2) Add the module in a Phase 2 project → (3) No change control needed for the current project

explanations.a: Implementing a change immediately because of the requester's seniority bypasses every governance step. The CIO's authority does not eliminate the need for impact assessment, budget authorization, or plan updates. A cybersecurity compliance module added to a 70%-complete project without analysis could blow the budget, delay delivery, or introduce technical debt.
explanations.b: Complete change control sequence for the CIO's cybersecurity module request: (1) CREATE/RECEIVE change request: formalize the CIO's verbal request into a written change request with description, justification, and preliminary scope; (2) DOCUMENT IN CHANGE CONTROL LOG: assign a CR ID; log date, requester (CIO), description, and 'Status: Submitted'; (3) PRELIMINARY REVIEW: is it in scope? is it technically feasible? is the request complete? At 70% completion, adding a new module is a significant late-stage change requiring full analysis; (4) IMPACT ASSESSMENT: schedule (+how many weeks?); cost (+how much for design, development, testing?); quality (does it require additional security testing cycles?); risk (integration risk with 70%-built system; schedule delay risk for other deliverables); resource (are cybersecurity SMEs available?); (5) DOCUMENT CHANGE RECOMMENDATION: PM prepares a recommendation with options (add in current project, add in Phase 2, reject); (6) DETERMINE DECISION MAKERS: at 70% completion, a significant new module likely exceeds PM and sponsor thresholds → CCB required; (7) CCB REVIEW AND DECISION: CCB evaluates the recommendation and decides; (8) LOG APPROVAL STATUS: update log to 'Approved/Rejected/Deferred' with decision rationale; (9) COMMUNICATE CHANGE STATUS: notify CIO, team, and relevant stakeholders; (10) UPDATE PROJECT PLAN: revise schedule, budget, resource plan, risk register; (11) IMPLEMENT CHANGES: team develops the compliance module; (12) VALIDATE: security testing, acceptance testing, compliance verification; (13) COMMUNICATE DEPLOYMENT: confirm module is live to CIO and all stakeholders.
explanations.c: There is no best practice rule prohibiting changes at 70% completion. Late-stage changes are discouraged because they are typically more expensive and disruptive, but they are not prohibited. A cybersecurity compliance module may be legally required (regulatory change) — making rejection inappropriate without analysis.
explanations.d: Deferring to Phase 2 without analysis may be the right recommendation (it's one of the options in the recommendation step), but it should emerge FROM the change control process, not replace it. Additionally, if the module is required for regulatory compliance, deferring it may not be legally permissible.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Change control process — project-specific change control tailoring
questions.text: A project manager is developing the change control plan for a 3-month fast-track software project with a small team of 5 people. Which change control approach is MOST appropriate for this project context?

answers.text: The same formal change control process used for an 18-month enterprise program — consistency in change control processes ensures organizational governance standards are met regardless of project size
No change control process — small projects with small teams do not need formal change control

A tailored lightweight change control process: simplified change request form (1 page); PM as the sole decision maker for changes within $2,000 and 2 days; sponsor for changes up to $10,000 and 1 week; a shared change log in a spreadsheet; decisions within 48 hours; emphasis on rapid communication
A verbal-only change control process — small teams can manage changes through daily stand-up discussions without any documentation

explanations.a: Applying full enterprise-program change control overhead (multi-week CCB cycles, extensive documentation, formal stage gates) to a 3-month, 5-person project would consume a disproportionate amount of the project's time and resources. Change control must be tailored to project size, complexity, and risk profile.
explanations.b: Small projects still experience scope creep, unauthorized additions, and uncontrolled changes. The absence of any change control — regardless of project size — leaves the project vulnerable to the same governance failures that derail large projects, just at smaller scale. A 3-month project can still fail from scope creep.
explanations.c: PROJECT-SPECIFIC CHANGE CONTROL means tailoring the process to fit the project's characteristics while maintaining governance integrity. For a 3-month, 5-person, fast-track project: Simplified form: a 1-page change request capturing the essential fields (description, justification, estimated impact) — not a 10-page enterprise template; Lower authority thresholds: the PM can approve small changes (within $2K, 2 days) without sponsor involvement — enabling fast decision-making; Electronic shared log: a shared spreadsheet is sufficient (a full-blown CMDB is overkill); Fast turnaround: 48-hour decision target maintains project momentum; Lightweight communication: a brief email or team update suffices (not a formal stakeholder communication package). This maintains: traceability (the log); governance (authority thresholds); communication (change status notifications); validation (confirming changes worked) — all scaled appropriately.
explanations.d: Verbal-only change control with no documentation fails the governance test: decisions are not traceable; there is no audit trail; team members may remember decisions differently; the log cannot be consulted to check whether a change was approved or rejected. Verbal discussions can SUPPLEMENT documentation but cannot REPLACE it.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Change control process — conduct impact assessments; product change vs. project change
questions.text: A project is building a customer data platform. A change request proposes replacing the planned on-premises data storage with a cloud-based data lake. The project manager must conduct a comprehensive impact assessment. Which FOUR impact dimensions are MOST critical to analyze for this specific change?

answers.text: Team morale, office space requirements, parking availability, and holiday scheduling

Technical architecture (migration from on-prem to cloud changes infrastructure design, APIs, security model); cost (cloud ongoing OpEx vs. one-time CapEx for on-prem; data transfer and egress costs); schedule (cloud provisioning, data migration, testing timeline); and compliance/security (data residency, encryption at rest/transit, GDPR/CCPA compliance for cloud-stored customer data)
Vendor preference, team technology familiarity, marketing messaging, and branding alignment with the company's cloud-first PR strategy
Only cost — the CFO needs to approve any change that switches from CapEx to OpEx

explanations.a: Team morale, office space, parking, and holiday scheduling are irrelevant to the technical, financial, and compliance impacts of switching from on-premises storage to a cloud data lake. These are not appropriate impact assessment dimensions for this change.
explanations.b: For an on-premises to cloud data lake migration change request, the four most critical impact dimensions are: (1) TECHNICAL ARCHITECTURE: The on-prem design (local servers, network topology, data access patterns, APIs connecting applications to storage) may be fundamentally different from a cloud data lake architecture (S3/ADLS/GCS, REST APIs, cloud-native access patterns, different latency characteristics). The entire data layer architecture may need redesign. (2) COST: Cloud vs. on-prem involves a fundamental financial model shift: On-prem: capital expenditure (CapEx) — servers, storage hardware, data center space — one-time large investment; Cloud: operational expenditure (OpEx) — monthly/annual subscription, data egress fees, API call costs — recurring smaller payments. The total cost of ownership (TCO) over the project/product lifetime must be analyzed. (3) SCHEDULE: Cloud provisioning is fast, but: the architecture changes require re-design time; existing on-prem data migration to cloud takes time; testing of cloud connectivity, latency, and failover adds to the schedule; security hardening of cloud configuration adds to the schedule. (4) COMPLIANCE/SECURITY: Customer data platforms store PII/customer data. Cloud storage of this data must comply with: data residency requirements (where is the data stored geographically?); GDPR, CCPA, and other privacy regulations; encryption requirements (at rest, in transit); access control model (IAM policies, least privilege); audit logging.
explanations.c: While cloud-first strategy alignment and team familiarity are valid contextual factors, they are secondary considerations compared to technical architecture, cost model, schedule, and regulatory compliance for a change of this magnitude.
explanations.d: Cost is the most visible impact but is insufficient alone. A cloud migration that is financially favorable but technically infeasible, compliance-violating, or schedule-busting cannot be approved based on cost analysis alone.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Change control process — document change recommendations; determine decision makers
questions.text: A project manager has completed the impact assessment for a change request to add a real-time inventory sync feature. The assessment shows: schedule +2 weeks, cost +$12,000, medium technical risk. The project manager now prepares the change recommendation. Which statement BEST describes a complete change recommendation?

answers.text: 'Recommend approval' — a one-line recommendation is sufficient because decision makers will review the impact assessment separately
'Recommend rejection due to cost' — the PM should always recommend rejection for any change that adds cost to the project

A structured recommendation presenting: summary of the change and its business justification; quantified impacts (schedule +2 weeks, cost +$12K, risk profile); 2-3 options with trade-offs (approve now; defer to Phase 2; reject); identified dependencies or constraints; PM's recommended option with clear rationale; and identification of who should make the final decision given the cost and schedule thresholds
A recommendation should not be prepared — the PM should present the impact assessment data and allow the decision maker to form their own recommendation without PM bias

explanations.a: A one-line recommendation without supporting context leaves the decision maker without the structured information needed to make a defensible decision. They would still need to review the entire impact assessment and form their own synthesis — wasting their time and failing to leverage the PM's analytical work.
explanations.b: Recommending rejection for any cost-adding change is a blanket policy that ignores strategic value. A $12,000 investment that delivers real-time inventory sync enabling $500,000 in annual savings is clearly worth approving despite the cost addition. The PM's role is objective analysis, not cost minimization.
explanations.c: A COMPLETE CHANGE RECOMMENDATION document packages all decision-relevant information for the decision maker: (1) Change summary: what the real-time inventory sync feature does and why the stakeholder wants it (business justification); (2) Quantified impacts: SCHEDULE: delivery delayed from March 1 to March 15 (+2 weeks); COST: $12,000 additional (broken down: $8,000 development, $2,500 testing, $1,500 infrastructure); RISK: medium technical risk (API integration with third-party inventory system — dependency on external vendor); (3) Options with trade-offs: Option A (Approve now): feature added, March 15 delivery, +$12K; Option B (Defer to Phase 2): no schedule/cost impact on current project; delivered in 2-month post-launch release; Option C (Reject): no cost or schedule impact; business loses real-time sync benefit; (4) PM Recommendation: 'We recommend Option B — defer to Phase 2 — because the March 1 deadline is contractually binding. The 2-week schedule slip would breach the SLA. The real-time sync can be delivered post-launch as Phase 2 without jeopardizing the primary delivery.' (5) Decision maker identification: 'Given the $12,000 cost addition, this decision requires sponsor approval per the change authority matrix.'
explanations.d: Presenting data without a recommendation fails to leverage the PM's analytical expertise and project knowledge. Decision makers rely on the PM for a synthesized recommendation — presenting raw data and deferring judgment is abdication, not neutrality.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Change control process — types of changes: scope, schedule, budget, quality
questions.text: Which of the following is NOT typically an example of a change request that requires formal change control?

answers.text: A request to add a new module to the project scope
A request to extend the project deadline by 3 weeks due to unexpected technical complexity
A team member updating their personal task notes in their project management tool
A request to increase the project budget by $50,000 to cover additional resource costs

explanations.a: Adding a new module to project scope is a SCOPE CHANGE — it modifies what the project will deliver. All scope changes require formal change control because they affect the scope baseline, which was formally approved at project initiation.
explanations.b: Extending the project deadline by 3 weeks is a SCHEDULE CHANGE — it modifies the schedule baseline. Schedule changes require formal change control, sponsor approval (at minimum), and updates to the project plan.
explanations.c: A team member updating their PERSONAL TASK NOTES (internal working notes, personal to-do lists, individual tracking records) does not change any project baseline, deliverable, scope, budget, or schedule. Personal task management is an individual work habit — not a project change that requires governance oversight. Change control applies to changes in the project's baselines and plans, not to individual team members' internal organization.
explanations.d: A $50,000 budget increase is a COST CHANGE — it modifies the cost baseline. Budget changes require formal change control, sponsor or CCB approval, and updates to the project budget baseline.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Change control process — escalate to CCB; CCB role and composition
questions.text: What is the PRIMARY function of the Change Control Board (CCB) in project management?

answers.text: To develop and write change requests on behalf of stakeholders who are too busy to submit them
To review, evaluate, and approve or reject change requests that exceed the project manager's or sponsor's authority level, providing governance over significant project changes
To implement approved changes by assigning specific team members to each change task
To replace the project manager when the project experiences too many change requests

explanations.a: The CCB does not develop or write change requests. Change requests originate from project stakeholders, team members, project managers, or sponsors — not the CCB. The CCB is a decision-making body, not a change request authoring service.
explanations.b: The CHANGE CONTROL BOARD (CCB) is a formally constituted group responsible for reviewing, evaluating, approving, delaying, or rejecting changes to the project. Key characteristics: GOVERNANCE BODY: the CCB provides authority-level decision-making for changes that exceed the project manager's or sponsor's defined thresholds; COMPOSITION: includes individuals with the authority and expertise to evaluate the change — typically the project sponsor, project manager, key stakeholders, technical leads, and subject matter experts relevant to the change; AUTHORITY: when the CCB approves a change, it is the highest-level organizational authorization within the project; ACCOUNTABILITY: CCB decisions are documented in the change control log with rationale; FREQUENCY: the CCB meets on a defined cadence (weekly, biweekly) or convenes on-demand for urgent changes.
explanations.c: Implementing approved changes is the responsibility of the project team — not the CCB. After the CCB approves a change, the project manager and team plan and execute the implementation. The CCB's role ends at the decision.
explanations.d: The CCB does not replace the project manager. The project manager remains responsible for managing the project, including facilitating the change control process and implementing CCB decisions. The CCB provides governance oversight, not day-to-day project management.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Change control process — manage scope change; baseline control
questions.text: A project sponsor calls the project manager to say: 'I know we're 8 weeks from go-live, but I need to add a regulatory reporting module. The CFO requires it for quarterly compliance.' The project manager must decide how to respond. What is the MOST appropriate course of action?

answers.text: Tell the sponsor the change cannot be made — regulatory requirements should have been identified during planning, so late additions are the sponsor's fault
Immediately assign the task to the development team — sponsor requests bypass change control

Acknowledge the regulatory requirement, initiate a formal change request, conduct an impact assessment to quantify the schedule and cost impact, present options (add in current project, fast-track with additional resources, defer to post-go-live patch), and escalate to the CCB given the late-stage significant scope addition
Tell the sponsor that regulatory requirements are out of scope and should be handled by the IT department as an operational change after the project closes

explanations.a: Telling the sponsor the change cannot be made and assigning blame is not constructive. Regulatory requirements can emerge late due to legislative changes, audit findings, or evolving compliance interpretations — the sponsor is not at fault for late-emerging regulatory requirements. The project manager's job is to solve problems, not assign blame.
explanations.b: Sponsor requests, regardless of seniority, do not bypass change control. Immediate implementation without impact assessment, plan update, and governance approval would violate project governance — and the team might spend weeks on the new module only to discover it is technically infeasible as described, or that it causes budget overruns the sponsor did not anticipate.
explanations.c: Regulatory requirements are high-priority change requests that warrant expedited but complete change control: ACKNOWLEDGE and validate the business need (regulatory compliance is typically non-optional); INITIATE a change request immediately; CONDUCT RAPID IMPACT ASSESSMENT: how many development weeks are needed (at 8 weeks to go-live, every week matters)?; what is the cost?; can the go-live date be maintained?; PRESENT OPTIONS: Option A (Add to current project): go-live delayed X weeks, cost +$Y; Option B (Fast-track with contract developers): go-live maintained, cost +$Z (significantly higher); Option C (Post-go-live patch): go-live maintained, regulatory module delivered within 30 days post-launch — does this satisfy the regulatory requirement's timing?; ESCALATE: a late-stage significant scope addition at 8 weeks to go-live likely requires CCB or sponsor decision with full business context.
explanations.d: Regulatory reporting required by the CFO for quarterly compliance cannot be deferred to 'the IT department as an operational change' — this minimizes the urgency and shifts accountability inappropriately. The project manager must engage with the change constructively.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Change control process — end-to-end process integration and tradeoffs
questions.text: A project manager reviews the change control log and finds: 8 approved changes, 3 rejected, 2 deferred, and 1 currently under review. The project is now 6 weeks behind schedule and 18% over budget. The project manager must report to the CCB. What MOST LIKELY caused the schedule and budget overrun, and what should the change control analysis reveal?

answers.text: The 3 rejected changes caused the overrun — rejected changes consume project resources before being declined
The 2 deferred changes are the problem — deferral always results in budget penalties

The cumulative impact of the 8 approved changes likely contributed significantly; the change control analysis should compare the cumulative approved change impacts (total schedule additions, total cost additions) to the current project variances to determine whether the changes were properly impact-assessed and whether the baselines were updated when changes were approved
The change currently under review is causing the overrun by consuming resources in limbo while awaiting CCB decision

explanations.a: Rejected changes should not consume significant project resources if the change control process is functioning correctly — rejected changes are identified and declined before implementation begins. If rejected changes are consuming resources, it suggests the team is implementing before approval (a process failure), not that rejection itself causes overruns.
explanations.b: Deferred changes are intentionally postponed — they do not consume current project resources. Deferral is a risk management tool, not a cost generator. Two deferred changes would not cause an 18% budget overrun.
explanations.c: Eight approved changes each adding schedule time and cost are the most likely contributors to the 6-week delay and 18% overrun. Change control analysis should reveal: CUMULATIVE CHANGE IMPACT: total approved schedule additions (sum of schedule impacts across 8 CRs); total approved cost additions (sum of cost impacts). If 8 changes each added 1 week to schedule: cumulative = 8 weeks → explains a 6-week delay (with partial mitigation). BASELINE UPDATE VERIFICATION: were the baselines updated when each change was approved? If the schedule baseline was never revised, the team has been executing against an outdated baseline — the 6-week 'overrun' may actually be planned (from approved changes) but not reflected in the reported baseline. RE-BASELINING NEED: if the cumulative approved changes justify the current position, the project needs a REVISED BASELINE, not a corrective action for overruns. RESIDUAL RISK: are future changes anticipated? What is the trend?
explanations.d: A change under review (not yet approved) should not be consuming implementation resources — the team should not begin implementation before approval. If they are, that is a change control process failure requiring correction, but it would typically have limited resource impact at the 'under review' stage.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Change control process — change status options: approve, reject, defer; scope management
questions.text: During a CCB meeting, a change request to add advanced reporting capabilities is evaluated. The CCB agrees the feature has high business value but determines that adding it now would delay the critical go-live date by 4 weeks, which would violate an SLA. The CCB decides to 'defer' the request. What does this mean and what should happen next?

answers.text: Defer means the change is permanently rejected — the CCB will never revisit it
Defer means the change is approved — the team should begin implementation immediately after the current sprint

Defer means the decision is postponed — the change request is not rejected, but it will not be implemented in the current project phase; it should be logged in the change control log as 'Deferred,' noted for consideration in the next project phase or release, and communicated to the requester with the rationale
Defer means the project manager should wait for the requester to resubmit — deferred changes are automatically deleted from the log

explanations.a: 'Deferred' is not the same as 'Rejected.' A rejected change has been evaluated and the CCB has decided it will not be implemented at all. A deferred change is acknowledged as valuable but is intentionally postponed — it may be reconsidered in the future.
explanations.b: 'Deferred' explicitly means the change is NOT being approved for the current phase. The team should NOT begin implementation of a deferred change. Deferral prevents the go-live SLA violation precisely by holding the change for a future release.
explanations.c: DEFERRED status in change control means: the change request has been evaluated; the CCB acknowledges its business value; the CCB has determined that the current project phase cannot accommodate the change without unacceptable impact (in this case, a 4-week SLA violation); the change is preserved for future consideration — typically the next project phase, next release, or a post-launch enhancement. Actions following deferral: UPDATE CHANGE LOG: status changed from 'Under Review' to 'Deferred'; document the deferral rationale; note the target release/phase for reconsideration; COMMUNICATE TO REQUESTER: explain the deferral decision and the planned timing for reconsideration; ROADMAP NOTE: the product owner (in Agile) or the project sponsor adds the deferred feature to the Phase 2 or post-launch roadmap; REVISIT at the next phase initiation: when planning Phase 2, the deferred change request should be reconsidered for inclusion.
explanations.d: Deferred changes remain in the change control log — they are not deleted. The log serves as a historical record of all change request activity. A deleted deferred change cannot be referenced during Phase 2 planning, creating the risk of re-submitting and re-assessing an already-analyzed change.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Change control process — product change vs. project change; scope creep; integrated change control
questions.text: A project manager audits the project at the 50% milestone and discovers: (1) The development team added 3 undocumented features based on developer judgment; (2) The project schedule was compressed 2 weeks without a change request because the sponsor 'verbally approved' the compression; (3) A formal change request to add a customer portal was approved by the CCB and is in progress. Classify each situation and identify the governance failures and appropriate corrective actions.

answers.text: All three situations are normal project management events — the audit is an overreaction to standard project execution flexibility
All three require retroactive CCB review — all project changes must pass through the CCB regardless of how they originated

Situation 1 (undocumented features): scope creep — unauthorized product changes; remove or retroactively submit change requests; reinforce team discipline. Situation 2 (verbal schedule compression): unauthorized project change — verbal approval is insufficient; submit a retroactive change request with documented impact; update the change log and schedule baseline. Situation 3 (approved customer portal CR): properly executed — this is change control working correctly; no corrective action needed

Situation 1: acceptable — developers have technical authority over features. Situation 2: acceptable — sponsor verbal approval is equivalent to written approval. Situation 3: excessive — the CCB process should be streamlined to avoid this much documentation
