explanations.c: COMPLETE ISSUE MANAGEMENT RESPONSE for a critical performance issue 4 days from go-live: (1) ISSUE LOG ENTRY: Issue #88: Trade confirmation delay >15 seconds under high concurrent load (>500 users); Severity: CRITICAL; Impact: SLA violation risk (contract requires <3 seconds); Urgency: CRITICAL (4 days to go-live); Org scope: all users, regulatory implications; Owner: infrastructure lead; (2) ROOT CAUSE ANALYSIS: database connection pool exhaustion identified as root cause — when >500 users execute simultaneous trades, the connection pool (currently sized for 200 connections) is exhausted; new requests queue, causing the 15-30 second delays; (3) DUAL-TRACK RESOLUTION: Track 1 WORKAROUND (2-hour fix): increase connection pool maximum from 200 to 800; reduce connection timeout from 30s to 5s to release idle connections faster; re-test under simulated 600-user load — validate <1 second confirmation; Track 2 PERMANENT FIX (post-launch, 2 weeks): optimize query efficiency to reduce connection hold time; implement connection pooling with async patterns; performance test to 1,000 concurrent users; (4) ESCALATE TO SPONSOR: options analysis (fix now + go-live on schedule / partial go-live with user cap / delay go-live); PM recommendation: implement workaround immediately, retest, go-live on schedule if workaround validates; (5) IMPLEMENT AND VALIDATE: increase pool, run load test at 600 concurrent users, verify <1s confirmations; (6) CHANGE REQUEST: CR-031 for permanent connection management refactoring — post-launch, 2-week timeline; (7) OUTCOME DOCUMENTATION: issue log closed with resolution details, test results, sponsor approval; risk register updated; (8) STAKEHOLDER COMMUNICATION: go-live status confirmed/adjusted based on workaround results.
explanations.d: A connection pool sizing fix is a configuration change, not an architectural re-design. Postponing 3 months for what is likely a 2-hour fix is disproportionate and would cause significant business harm (contract penalties, lost trading revenue, competitor advantage).

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Issue management — issue tracking log; issue status management; resolution tracking
questions.text: A project manager is reviewing the issue log at the weekly status meeting. Three issues are marked 'In Progress' with the same owner for 3 consecutive weeks, and no updates have been posted to any of them. The owner is present at the meeting. What is the MOST appropriate action?

answers.text: Remove the owner from the team — three weeks without updates indicates willful negligence
Close all three issues — if no progress has been documented in 3 weeks, the issues are no longer relevant

Request a status update from the owner immediately; if the issues are genuinely blocked, identify blockers and either resolve them or escalate; update the issue log with current status, revised target dates if necessary, and the escalation path; set a re-review date for next week
Transfer all three issues to a different owner — the current owner is clearly unable to handle the workload

explanations.a: Three weeks without log updates may indicate poor documentation habits, blocked progress, unclear ownership expectations, or workload overload — not necessarily 'willful negligence.' Removing a team member without understanding the situation is a disproportionate response.
explanations.b: Issues that have been open for 3 weeks with no visible progress are not 'no longer relevant' — they may be growing in impact. Closing them without resolution removes them from visibility and oversight.
explanations.c: ISSUE REVIEW ACTION at the weekly meeting: IMMEDIATE STATUS REQUEST: 'John, let's discuss the status of Issues #12, #15, and #18 — they've been in progress for 3 weeks with no log updates. Can you give us a current status?' POSSIBLE SCENARIOS and responses: (a) Owner has been working on them but not updating the log → remind of log maintenance requirements; request immediate log updates with current status; (b) Owner is blocked → identify the specific blockers (technical: need SME help; organizational: awaiting a decision; resource: lacks time due to other priorities); resolve blockers or escalate; (c) Owner has not made progress due to workload → assess workload; consider reassigning or adding support; (d) Issues are actually resolved → owner updates log with closure documentation immediately. ACTIONS: update log with current status today (meeting outcome); set revised target resolution dates; set next review date (1 week); determine if escalation is needed. This approach is direct, constructive, and maintains team accountability without being punitive.
explanations.d: Transferring ownership without understanding why progress has stalled may not solve the underlying problem. If the issues are technically blocked, a new owner will hit the same wall. Understanding the blockers comes first.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Issue management — issue tracking log; issue status updates; project health indicator
questions.text: A project manager inherits a project and reviews the issue log. They find 23 issues marked 'In Progress' with target dates ranging from 2 to 8 months ago — all dates have passed. None of the issues have been escalated or closed. What does this issue log indicate about project health, and what immediate actions are required?

answers.text: The project is healthy — many open issues indicate active project work

The issue log is out of date and the project is likely in trouble; immediate actions: audit each issue to determine current true status; close resolved issues with outcome documentation; escalate issues that are genuinely blocked; update target dates for issues still in progress; brief the sponsor on the current issue backlog and project health
All 23 issues should be immediately closed to give the new PM a fresh start
The previous PM was negligent — file a formal complaint and request an independent audit

explanations.a: Twenty-three open issues with target dates 2-8 months expired is a strong indicator of project distress, not health. Active projects do have open issues, but unresolved, unescalated, past-due issues indicate a breakdown in issue management governance.
explanations.b: An expired-date-heavy issue log indicates: GOVERNANCE FAILURE: no escalation triggers when dates were missed; no PM-level review of issue currency; POTENTIAL PROJECT DISTRESS: issues that should have been resolved months ago may be creating cascading impacts on schedule, budget, and quality; INFORMATION VACUUM: the new PM cannot make informed decisions without knowing which of the 23 issues are genuine open problems vs. already resolved but not documented. IMMEDIATE ACTIONS: (1) AUDIT each issue: contact each owner individually; determine true status (resolved, blocked, still in progress); (2) CLOSE resolved issues: document resolution outcomes for issues that are actually done — many 'in progress' issues may have been resolved without log updates; (3) ESCALATE genuine blockers: for issues that are genuinely unresolved due to organizational, resource, or technical blockers — escalate to the sponsor with urgency; (4) UPDATE target dates: for issues still actively in progress — set realistic new target dates; (5) BRIEF THE SPONSOR: provide an honest current-state assessment of the issue backlog; identify the highest-severity open issues; develop a remediation plan with the sponsor's support.
explanations.c: Closing all 23 issues without audit creates a false picture of project health and destroys the governance record. Resolved issues need closure documentation; unresolved issues cannot be closed without resolution.
explanations.d: While a formal complaint may eventually be warranted depending on findings, the immediate priority is restoring project governance — not administrative action. The new PM's first obligation is to understand and stabilize the project's current state.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Issue management — connections between issues and risks; risk register update after issue resolution
questions.text: A project team resolves a critical issue (production database migration failure) using the pre-planned contingency plan. The issue is formally closed in the issue log. What should happen to the related risk register entry (Risk #7: 'Database migration may fail during cutover') now that the risk has materialized and been resolved?

answers.text: Nothing — the risk register is only used before the project starts; it does not need to be updated after risks materialize
Delete Risk #7 from the risk register — resolved risks should be removed to keep the register current

Update Risk #7 in the risk register: change status to 'Occurred/Resolved'; document that the contingency plan was activated and was successful; cross-reference Issue log entry; note any residual risk (e.g., data integrity validation still needed); update lessons learned; retain the entry for audit trail and future project reference
Move Risk #7 to a 'Lessons Learned' document and remove it from the active risk register — risks that occurred are historical facts, not active risks

explanations.a: The risk register is a living document maintained throughout the project lifecycle — including during and after risk events occur. Failing to update it when risks materialize creates an inaccurate view of the risk landscape.
explanations.b: Deleting Risk #7 destroys the audit trail. The risk register documents the organization's risk management decisions and effectiveness. Evidence that Risk #7 was identified, planned for, and successfully resolved through a contingency plan is valuable: for auditors verifying risk management governance; for future project teams facing similar risks who can see the contingency plan worked; for the PMO tracking risk management effectiveness across projects.
explanations.c: RISK REGISTER UPDATE after a risk materializes and is resolved: STATUS UPDATE: change from 'Active/Monitored' to 'Occurred → Resolved'; CONTINGENCY EFFECTIVENESS: document that Risk #7's contingency plan (database rollback procedure) was activated and successfully resolved the migration failure; this validates the contingency planning investment; CROSS-REFERENCE: link Risk #7 to Issue Log entry #28 (database migration failure) — complete traceability; RESIDUAL RISK: even though the migration failed and was recovered, are there residual concerns? (data integrity validation still pending? migration retry scheduled? any known data gaps from the failed migration?); LESSONS LEARNED: what worked? what could be improved in the contingency plan? (e.g., the rollback took 45 minutes instead of the planned 20 minutes — update the plan for next time); RETENTION: the entry remains in the register but with 'Occurred/Resolved' status — visible for audit and lessons-learned purposes.
explanations.d: Moving to a lessons-learned document while removing from the risk register creates a split record — auditors looking at the risk register don't see that the risk occurred; people reading lessons learned may not connect it to the risk register entry. The risk register should contain the complete risk history including outcomes, cross-referenced to lessons learned.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Issue management — complete lifecycle: identification through closure; all key connections
questions.text: A project manager receives the following from different team members in one morning: (A) Developer: 'The API endpoint returns a 403 error for all requests authenticated with OAuth tokens — blocks our entire testing phase.' (B) BA: 'The client wants to add a new dashboard screen — it's not in scope but they're saying it's urgent.' (C) Tester: 'We discovered that the product catalog displays prices without tax in Germany but German law requires tax-inclusive prices.' (D) Scrum master: 'We're 3 story points behind our sprint goal and it's Day 8 of a 10-day sprint.' Classify each item (issue/change request/risk/sprint problem) and identify the correct management response for each.

answers.text: All four are issues — log them all in the issue log and assign owners
All four are change requests — all project problems require a formal change request to address

(A) Issue: API 403 error → log in issue log (HIGH severity, blocks testing), assign owner, initiate root cause investigation, implement workaround if available; (B) Change request: client wants out-of-scope dashboard → direct client to submit formal change request, conduct impact assessment if submitted; (C) Issue requiring change: German tax display → log as compliance issue (HIGH/CRITICAL), investigate root cause (hard-coded vs. locale logic), initiate change request to fix the tax display logic; (D) Sprint performance indicator: 3 story points behind on Day 8 → raise in daily stand-up, discuss sprint goal achievability with team, consider scope reduction (drop lowest-priority story), address in retrospective

(A) Risk — the API may fail again in the future; (B) Issue — the client's request is a current problem; (C) Risk — German tax law may change; (D) Change request — the sprint goal needs a formal change request to modify

explanations.a: Not all four are issues. Item B (client requesting out-of-scope feature) is a CHANGE REQUEST — a proposed scope addition. Item D (sprint performance) is a sprint management situation, not a formal issue requiring issue log documentation. Over-logging creates noise in the issue register.
explanations.b: Not all four are change requests. Items A and C are current problems (issues) that need immediate resolution. Item D is a sprint execution metric, not a change to be formally requested.
explanations.c: Correct classification and response: (A) API 403 ERROR → ISSUE: A current, active problem blocking testing. Issue log entry: HIGH severity (critical path blocker); owner: API integration lead; target: resolve within 24 hours (testing phase blocked); root cause: OAuth token configuration mismatch (likely); immediate workaround: use API keys temporarily while OAuth is fixed. (B) CLIENT OUT-OF-SCOPE DASHBOARD → CHANGE REQUEST: the client's request is a proposed scope addition — it does not belong in the issue log. Response: acknowledge the request professionally; explain the change control process; request formal CR submission; conduct impact assessment when submitted; do not do any work on the dashboard until the CR is approved. (C) GERMAN TAX DISPLAY → ISSUE REQUIRING CHANGE: a compliance issue (hard legal requirement) that will require remediation work. Log as compliance issue in the issue log (CRITICAL — legal violation risk, affects all German users); initiate root cause analysis (is it hard-coded EUR price, or does locale/tax configuration logic not exist?); depending on root cause, a change request for the fix may be needed (if fixing requires scope addition); severity and urgency are HIGH — tax compliance is non-negotiable. (D) SPRINT PERFORMANCE → SPRINT MANAGEMENT (not a formal issue): 3 story points behind on Day 8 of 10 is a sprint delivery risk. Address in daily stand-up: is the sprint goal still achievable? Options: team accelerates (pair programming on remaining stories); drop the lowest-priority story to protect sprint goal; address scope reduction with product owner. If the sprint goal is genuinely at risk, address in retrospective.
explanations.d: This classification has multiple errors: the API error is a current problem (issue), not a risk. The client's out-of-scope request is a change request, not an issue. German tax law not changing is not the relevant risk — the TAX DISPLAY IS CURRENTLY WRONG (issue). The sprint performance does not require a change request — it's managed within the sprint through the agile process.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Quality & performance management — KPIs (key performance indicators); OKRs; SLA
questions.text: A project manager tracks the following metric: 'Percentage of sprint stories completed by their committed deadline.' This is BEST classified as:

answers.text: A key performance indicator (KPI) — it is a measurable value used to evaluate how effectively the project team is achieving a key objective (on-time story delivery)
A service-level agreement (SLA) — it defines the minimum acceptable service level between the project team and the client
An objective and key result (OKR) — it defines the objective the team is trying to reach and the specific outcome being measured
A schedule variance (SV) — it measures the difference between earned value and planned value

explanations.a: A KEY PERFORMANCE INDICATOR (KPI) is a quantifiable measurement used to evaluate the success of an organization, project, or team in achieving key objectives. 'Percentage of sprint stories completed by their committed deadline' is a KPI because: it is measurable (percentage); it tracks a specific outcome the team values (predictable delivery); it provides actionable insight (low % = process problems; high % = reliable team); it supports performance management decisions. KPIs are used for internal team performance monitoring, not external contractual commitments.
explanations.b: An SLA is a formal agreement between a service provider and a client specifying the minimum performance standards (e.g., system uptime ≥99.9%, response time <3 seconds). It is a contractual commitment, not an internal project performance measurement metric.
explanations.c: An OKR (Objective and Key Result) is a goal-setting framework with two components: the Objective (qualitative, aspirational direction — 'Deliver a high-quality product on schedule') and the Key Results (quantitative, specific outcomes — 'Achieve 90% of stories completed by deadline in every sprint'). The metric described is a Key Result measurement — it's part of an OKR, but by itself it is the measurement tool (KPI), not the full OKR framework.
explanations.d: Schedule Variance (SV) is a specific earned value management formula: SV = Earned Value (EV) − Planned Value (PV). It produces a dollar value, not a percentage. The metric described does not use earned value calculations.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Quality & performance management — service-level agreement (SLA); performance standards
questions.text: A client contract states: 'The delivered system must maintain 99.5% uptime during business hours and respond to 95% of API requests within 500 milliseconds.' This statement is BEST described as:

answers.text: A service-level agreement (SLA) — a contractual commitment defining the minimum acceptable performance standards the system must meet
A project KPI — these are the performance indicators the project team will track during development
A quality audit criterion — these standards are used only during formal quality audits
A schedule milestone — 99.5% uptime and 500ms response time define when the project is complete

explanations.a: A SERVICE-LEVEL AGREEMENT (SLA) is a formal contractual document (or clause within a contract) that specifies the minimum performance standards a service or system must meet, typically including: availability/uptime requirements (99.5% during business hours); performance/response time requirements (95% of API requests <500ms); support response times; data recovery objectives; measurement methods; consequences for non-compliance (financial penalties, service credits). SLAs are quality acceptance criteria — the project team must build and test the system to meet these standards, and the client will measure ongoing compliance post-delivery.
explanations.b: KPIs are internal performance measurement tools used by the project team to monitor progress. The uptime and response time requirements are CONTRACTUAL standards the delivered system must meet — externally imposed, not internal team measurements.
explanations.c: Quality audits verify that quality processes are being followed — they use standards like SLAs as evaluation criteria but are not the SLA itself.
explanations.d: Schedule milestones mark specific delivery points in time (e.g., 'UAT complete by March 1'). Performance standards like uptime and response time are quality/acceptance criteria, not schedule milestones.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Quality & performance management — unit testing; smoke testing; regression testing
questions.text: After deploying a new build, the QA team runs a quick 15-minute check to verify that the application launches, users can log in, and the main navigation works — before starting full testing. This quick validation is BEST described as:

answers.text: Regression testing — verifying that previously working features still work after the new build
User acceptance testing (UAT) — end users are verifying the system meets their needs
Performance testing — measuring how quickly the application launches and navigation loads
Smoke testing — a fast, shallow test to determine whether the build is stable enough to warrant further detailed testing

explanations.a: Regression testing is comprehensive testing of previously working functionality to ensure a new change has not broken existing features. It is thorough, systematic, and time-consuming — not a quick 15-minute check. Regression testing would cover all previously validated features, not just basic launch and login.
explanations.b: UAT is performed by the actual end users or business stakeholders to validate that the system meets business requirements. A QA team running a quick technical launch verification is not UAT.
explanations.c: Performance testing measures system behavior under various load conditions (response times, throughput, resource utilization). A check that navigation 'works' is a functional test, not a performance measurement.
explanations.d: SMOKE TESTING (also called 'build verification testing' or 'sanity testing') is a rapid, high-level test to determine if the basic build is viable enough to proceed with full testing. Origin: named after the practice of turning on electronics and checking if 'smoke comes out' (catastrophic failure). Characteristics: fast (15-30 minutes); covers only critical basic functionality (can it launch? can users authenticate? do the most essential workflows respond?); binary outcome (pass = proceed to full testing; fail = return build to development for fixes); prevents wasting the full QA team's time on a fundamentally broken build.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Quality & performance management — verification and validation
questions.text: A project team builds a login feature. During internal quality review, the QA engineer confirms the login module was coded exactly according to the technical specification. Later, the product owner reviews the feature and confirms that users can log in the way the business actually needed. Which quality activities are being described?

answers.text: The QA engineer's review is verification (built it right — matches the specification); the product owner's review is validation (built the right thing — meets actual business need)
Both are validation — both are checking that the system works correctly
The QA engineer's review is validation; the product owner's review is verification
Both are verification — comparing against a written specification is always verification

explanations.a: The classic distinction: VERIFICATION: 'Are we building the product RIGHT?' Did we build what the specifications say? Did we follow the design correctly? Does the code match the technical requirement? The QA engineer checks the login module against the technical specification — verifying that the implementation matches what was designed. Verification can catch: coding errors, implementation deviations, specification non-compliance. VALIDATION: 'Are we building the RIGHT product?' Does what we built actually meet the customer's real need? Will users find it useful? Does it solve the business problem it was intended to solve? The product owner confirms users can log in as the business needed — validating that the feature meets actual business requirements, not just technical specifications. Validation can catch: requirements that were incomplete, misunderstood, or that don't reflect actual user needs. IMPORTANT GAP: a system can PASS verification (built exactly to spec) but FAIL validation (the spec didn't capture what users actually needed). Both activities are necessary.
explanations.b: The two quality activities serve fundamentally different purposes and should be distinguished to understand what each one catches and misses.
explanations.c: This is reversed. The QA engineer checking against a specification is verification (matching spec = right way?). The product owner confirming business need is validation (meets actual need = right thing?).
explanations.d: Only the QA engineer's specification-comparison activity is verification. The product owner's business-need confirmation is validation.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Quality & performance management — cost variance (CV); schedule variance (SV); performance measurement
questions.text: A project has: Planned Value (PV) = $80,000; Earned Value (EV) = $70,000; Actual Cost (AC) = $85,000. Calculate the Cost Variance (CV) and Schedule Variance (SV), and interpret what they indicate.

answers.text: CV = −$15,000 (EV − AC = $70,000 − $85,000; negative = over budget); SV = −$10,000 (EV − PV = $70,000 − $80,000; negative = behind schedule)
CV = $10,000 (positive — under budget); SV = $15,000 (positive — ahead of schedule)
CV = $15,000 (AC − EV; positive = savings); SV = $10,000 (PV − EV; positive = efficiency)
CV = −$10,000; SV = −$5,000 — the variances are the average of all three values

explanations.a: Earned Value Management (EVM) formulas: COST VARIANCE (CV) = EV − AC = $70,000 − $85,000 = −$15,000. INTERPRETATION: CV is NEGATIVE → the project is OVER BUDGET. The project has spent $85,000 (AC) to accomplish work valued at $70,000 (EV) — spending $15,000 more than the work is worth. SCHEDULE VARIANCE (SV) = EV − PV = $70,000 − $80,000 = −$10,000. INTERPRETATION: SV is NEGATIVE → the project is BEHIND SCHEDULE. The project has accomplished $70,000 worth of planned work (EV) but was supposed to have accomplished $80,000 worth by now (PV) — behind by $10,000 in planned value. Summary: this project is simultaneously OVER BUDGET and BEHIND SCHEDULE — a double negative that requires immediate attention and corrective action.
explanations.b: Positive CV and SV would indicate under budget and ahead of schedule — the opposite of this project's situation. The formulas are CV = EV − AC and SV = EV − PV.
explanations.c: The formulas are inverted. CV = EV − AC (not AC − EV) and SV = EV − PV (not PV − EV). The sign of the variance (positive = favorable, negative = unfavorable) is determined by whether EV is larger or smaller than the comparison value.
explanations.d: EVM variances are not averages — they are specific formulas with defined meanings. CV = EV − AC; SV = EV − PV. There is no averaging calculation.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Quality & performance management — OKRs (objectives and key results); goal-setting and measurement
questions.text: A project team sets the following goal: Objective: 'Deliver a high-performance e-commerce platform that delights customers.' Key Results: (KR1) System uptime ≥99.9% for 90 days post-launch; (KR2) 95% of customer transactions complete in <2 seconds; (KR3) Customer satisfaction score ≥4.2 out of 5.0 at 30-day post-launch survey. The project manager asks: 'Are these good OKRs?' Evaluate the quality of this OKR structure.

answers.text: Good OKRs — the objective is inspirational and qualitative (direction-setting); the key results are specific, measurable, time-bound outcomes that define what 'delights customers' means in concrete terms; each KR can be objectively scored to determine if the objective was achieved
Poor OKRs — objectives should be numerical and key results should be qualitative to balance the framework
Poor OKRs — key results should only measure internal team process metrics (like sprint velocity), not customer-facing outcomes
Good OKRs — but they should also include a budget objective as a fourth key result to make them complete

explanations.a: QUALITY OKR EVALUATION: OBJECTIVE: 'Deliver a high-performance e-commerce platform that delights customers' — Qualitative ✓; Aspirational and direction-setting ✓; Memorable and meaningful ✓; Not easily measured directly (which is why KRs are needed) ✓. KEY RESULT 1 (Uptime ≥99.9%): Specific ✓; Measurable (monitoring tools) ✓; Time-bound (90 days post-launch) ✓; Directly tied to 'high-performance' ✓. KEY RESULT 2 (<2 second transactions): Specific ✓; Measurable (performance testing, APM tools) ✓; Directly tied to 'high-performance' ✓. KEY RESULT 3 (Satisfaction ≥4.2/5.0): Specific ✓; Measurable (survey) ✓; Time-bound (30 days post-launch) ✓; Directly tied to 'delights customers' ✓. These are well-formed OKRs — they pass the 'SMART Key Results' test and together operationalize what success means for the objective.
explanations.b: This is reversed. In the OKR framework: OBJECTIVES should be QUALITATIVE — inspiring, directional, motivating ('delight customers' is aspirational and direction-setting); KEY RESULTS should be QUANTITATIVE — specific, measurable, achievable, and time-bound (the numbers that define success).
explanations.c: Key results can and should measure customer-facing outcomes — the entire purpose of 'key results' is to define what success looks like from the customer's perspective, not just internal process metrics. OKRs that measure only internal processes can produce efficient teams delivering the wrong thing.
explanations.d: Adding a budget KR would make these OKRs into a management dashboard metric set, not an OKR. OKRs should focus on the most important 3-5 outcomes — including every possible metric dilutes focus. Budget management is separate from the product quality OKR.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Quality & performance management — contingency reserves/buffer utilization; reserve management
questions.text: A project has a $500,000 budget with $50,000 in contingency reserves (10%). At the 50% milestone, the project has spent $280,000 in direct costs and has used $30,000 of the contingency reserve. The original contingency plan anticipated that by 50% completion, approximately $20,000 of reserves would have been used. How should the project manager interpret this and what action is appropriate?

answers.text: No action needed — using $30,000 of reserves at 50% is within the original plan and reserves are meant to be used
Immediately cancel the project — using any contingency reserves indicates the project is out of control
Transfer the remaining $20,000 of contingency reserve to the project budget to ensure the budget baseline is met

CONTINGENCY RESERVE BURN RATE is elevated: $30,000 used vs. $20,000 planned at 50% completion means reserves are depleting 50% faster than anticipated; the project manager should investigate what risks triggered the additional $10,000 in reserve use, update the risk register, and assess whether the remaining $20,000 of reserves is sufficient to cover anticipated risks for the remaining 50% of the project

explanations.a: $30,000 used vs. $20,000 planned = 50% more contingency consumption than anticipated. This is not 'within plan' — it is a 50% overrun in reserve utilization rate. If this rate continues, the project will exhaust all $50,000 in reserves by approximately the 83% completion mark, leaving no reserve for the remaining 17% of work.
explanations.b: Using contingency reserves is expected and appropriate — that is their purpose. The issue is not that reserves were used, but that they were used at a HIGHER RATE than planned. Projects without any reserve usage often indicate over-conservative planning, not necessarily better execution.
explanations.c: Moving contingency reserves to the budget baseline changes the financial baseline without proper change control authorization. Contingency reserves are specifically kept separate from the budget baseline — their use requires PM authorization under the risk management plan.
explanations.d: CONTINGENCY RESERVE BURN RATE analysis: PLANNED: $20,000 used by 50% completion (2.0% of budget used as reserves at midpoint). ACTUAL: $30,000 used by 50% completion ($10,000 overrun = 50% higher burn rate than planned). REMAINING RESERVES: $50,000 − $30,000 = $20,000. PROJECTION: if the burn rate continues at the same pace, the project needs approximately $20,000 more in reserves for the remaining 50% of work — exactly equal to remaining reserves, with no margin. ACTION: (1) Investigate what risks triggered the additional $10,000 (risk register review); (2) Reassess the remaining risks — are any risks now more likely given the project's current state?; (3) Update the risk register probability/impact scores; (4) Assess whether the remaining $20,000 is sufficient or if management reserve should be requested; (5) Brief the sponsor on the contingency utilization trend.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Quality & performance management — retrospective/lessons learned; sprint review; continuous improvement
questions.text: At the end of Sprint 4, a Scrum team holds two meetings. In the first, the development team demonstrates the completed features to the product owner and stakeholders, who provide feedback. In the second, just the Scrum team (Scrum master + developers + product owner) discusses what went well, what didn't, and what to change for Sprint 5. Which meetings are these?

answers.text: The first is the sprint review; the second is the sprint retrospective — the review evaluates WHAT was built; the retrospective evaluates HOW the team is working
Both are retrospectives — all end-of-sprint meetings are retrospectives in Scrum
The first is the retrospective; the second is the sprint review — demonstrations always happen after the team reflects
Both are sprint planning meetings — end-of-sprint meetings focus on planning the next sprint

explanations.a: SPRINT REVIEW (first meeting): PURPOSE: inspect the increment (what was built) and adapt the product backlog; ATTENDEES: Scrum team + stakeholders + product owner; CONTENT: team demonstrates working software; product owner accepts/rejects items; stakeholders provide feedback; backlog may be adapted based on feedback; OUTCOME: updated product backlog reflecting current priorities and new information. SPRINT RETROSPECTIVE (second meeting): PURPOSE: inspect the process (how the team works) and create a plan for improvement; ATTENDEES: Scrum team only (Scrum master, developers, product owner — NOT external stakeholders); CONTENT: what went well? (strengths to preserve); what didn't go well? (problems to address); what specific changes will be made in Sprint 5?; OUTCOME: actionable improvement items added to the next sprint's plan. Key distinction: Sprint Review = WHAT did we build? Sprint Retrospective = HOW did we build it and how can we improve?
explanations.b: Scrum has two distinct end-of-sprint events with different purposes. Treating both as 'retrospectives' conflates the product inspection purpose (sprint review) with the process improvement purpose (retrospective).
explanations.c: The sequence in Scrum is: Sprint Review first (evaluate the product) → Sprint Retrospective second (evaluate the process). The demonstration of working software (Review) logically precedes the process reflection (Retrospective).
explanations.d: Sprint Planning occurs at the BEGINNING of a sprint, not the end. Sprint planning selects and plans work for the upcoming sprint. End-of-sprint events are the review and retrospective.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Quality & performance management — unit testing; test plan and testing cycles
questions.text: A developer writes a function that calculates the discounted price for a product. She writes a test that calls the function with a price of $100 and a 20% discount, and verifies the result is $80. She also tests with a 0% discount (expects $100) and a 100% discount (expects $0). This testing approach is BEST described as:

answers.text: Integration testing — the function is being tested as part of the larger system
User acceptance testing — the tests are verifying the business requirement for discounts
Regression testing — the tests verify that the discount function has not been broken by previous code changes
Unit testing — individual, isolated functions or components are tested in isolation with controlled inputs and verified against expected outputs

explanations.a: Integration testing tests how multiple components or systems work TOGETHER — for example, testing how the discount function interacts with the shopping cart, which interacts with the inventory system. The developer is testing only the single discount function in isolation, not integrations between components.
explanations.b: UAT is performed by business stakeholders or end users to validate that the system meets business needs — not by developers testing specific functions in code. The developer is conducting technical verification, not business validation.
explanations.c: Regression testing re-runs tests (often including unit tests) after a code change to verify that previously working functionality has not been broken. The developer is writing NEW tests for a NEW function — this is initial unit testing, not re-testing previously verified functionality.
explanations.d: UNIT TESTING tests the SMALLEST testable units of code (individual functions, methods, or modules) in ISOLATION from the rest of the system. Characteristics: written and executed by developers (often before or alongside the code itself in TDD); tests a single function/method with known inputs; verifies the output matches the expected result; runs fast (milliseconds); provides immediate feedback during development; helps catch bugs at the earliest, cheapest stage. The developer testing the discount function with multiple input combinations (boundary testing: 0%, 20%, 100%) is textbook unit testing.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Quality & performance management — regression testing; impact of changes on existing functionality
questions.text: A development team adds a new payment method (cryptocurrency) to an existing e-commerce platform. The testing team then re-runs all previously passed tests for the existing payment methods (credit card, PayPal, bank transfer) to ensure the cryptocurrency addition has not broken them. This testing is BEST described as:

answers.text: User acceptance testing — the business is verifying all payment methods work for customers
Smoke testing — a quick check that the basic build is still functional after the new payment method was added
Performance testing — verifying that the new payment method does not slow down existing payment processing
Regression testing — re-running previously validated tests after a code change to confirm that the new addition has not broken existing functionality

explanations.a: UAT is performed by business stakeholders or end users to validate business requirements, not by the testing team re-running technical test suites. UAT would occur after regression testing confirms existing functionality still works.
explanations.b: Smoke testing is a quick, shallow check of basic functionality (can the application launch? can users log in?) — not a comprehensive re-run of all previously passed tests for specific functional areas.
explanations.c: Performance testing measures system behavior under load (response times, throughput, resource consumption). Re-running existing functional tests for payment methods is functional/regression testing, not performance measurement.
explanations.d: REGRESSION TESTING is the process of re-executing tests that previously passed to verify that recent code changes (adding cryptocurrency payments) have not introduced defects in previously working functionality. Why regression is needed: adding new code can unintentionally affect existing code through: shared libraries or functions; database schema changes; API contract modifications; configuration changes affecting all payment methods. Without regression testing, a cryptocurrency addition could silently break credit card processing — a critical defect that might only be discovered when a customer's purchase fails in production. Regression test suites are typically automated to make re-execution fast and consistent.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Quality & performance management — stress testing; performance testing; differences between test types
questions.text: A QA team subjects a web application to increasingly heavy user loads until the application fails, then monitors how the system behaves during the failure and how it recovers when load is reduced. The goal is to understand the system's breaking point and recovery behavior. This testing is BEST described as:

answers.text: Stress testing — pushing the system beyond its normal operational limits to identify its breaking point, failure mode, and recovery capability
Performance testing — testing the system under expected load conditions to measure response times
Regression testing — verifying the system still works correctly after the load is removed
User acceptance testing — end users are validating that the system can handle real-world load

explanations.a: STRESS TESTING deliberately pushes the system BEYOND its normal operational limits to: (1) IDENTIFY THE BREAKING POINT: at what load level does the system fail? (2) OBSERVE FAILURE MODE: does the system fail gracefully (degraded but functional) or catastrophically (crash, data corruption, unresponsive)? (3) TEST RECOVERY: does the system recover automatically when load is reduced? How long does recovery take? Is data integrity preserved during recovery? Stress testing is critical for: systems with variable load (e-commerce during sales events); high-availability systems where graceful degradation is required; systems where failure mode matters (bank systems must never corrupt data even under extreme load). Stress testing knowledge enables: capacity planning; failover configuration; alerting thresholds; DR activation triggers.
explanations.b: Performance testing measures system behavior under EXPECTED, NORMAL load conditions — how fast is it? does it meet SLA response times? does it handle anticipated concurrent users? The test described deliberately pushes BEYOND normal conditions to find the breaking point — this is stress testing, not performance testing.
explanations.c: Regression testing re-runs previously passed tests after code changes — it is not about monitoring recovery from load. The test described is evaluating failure behavior and recovery under extreme conditions.
explanations.d: UAT is performed by end users to validate business requirements — not by QA teams deliberately overloading systems to find breaking points.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Quality & performance management — performance testing; SLA validation; stress vs. performance
questions.text: The SLA for a new claims processing system requires: 'System shall process 1,000 claims per hour with average processing time <4 seconds per claim under peak load.' The testing team executes a test generating 1,000 simultaneous claim submissions and measures processing times. This is BEST described as:

answers.text: Stress testing — the system is being pushed to find its breaking point
Smoke testing — a quick initial check that claim processing works
Unit testing — testing each individual claim processing function in isolation
Performance testing — measuring whether the system meets its specified performance requirements (SLA) under defined load conditions

explanations.a: Stress testing pushes BEYOND normal operational limits to find the breaking point. The test described is validating performance at the DEFINED PEAK LOAD (1,000 claims/hour — the expected maximum, not a system-breaking load). The purpose is SLA validation, not breaking point identification.
explanations.b: Smoke testing is a fast, shallow check of basic functionality. Processing 1,000 simultaneous claim submissions is a full-scale, resource-intensive performance validation — not a quick sanity check.
explanations.c: Unit testing tests individual code functions in isolation — not 1,000 simultaneous end-to-end claim processing operations.
explanations.d: PERFORMANCE TESTING measures system behavior under defined load conditions to verify that performance requirements (SLA) are met. In this case: LOAD: 1,000 simultaneous claims (the defined peak load from the SLA); MEASUREMENT: average processing time per claim; TARGET: <4 seconds per claim; OUTCOME: pass (meets SLA) or fail (does not meet SLA, requires optimization). Performance testing encompasses: load testing (defined expected load); stress testing (beyond normal limits); spike testing (sudden load surges); endurance/soak testing (sustained load over extended periods). This specific test is a LOAD TEST — a subset of performance testing that validates the system meets SLA at the defined peak load.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Quality & performance management — user acceptance testing (UAT); business validation
questions.text: After the QA team completes all technical testing cycles, 15 actual HR department employees spend two weeks using the new payroll system with real (anonymized) pay scenarios to confirm the system meets HR's actual business workflows. Which type of testing is this, and what is its PRIMARY purpose?

answers.text: Regression testing — HR is verifying that no existing payroll calculations were broken during development
Performance testing — HR is evaluating whether the system processes payroll fast enough for their needs
Smoke testing — HR's initial use of the system confirms the basic build is stable
User acceptance testing (UAT) — actual end users validate that the system meets real business requirements, workflows, and usability standards, and formally accept or reject the system for deployment

explanations.a: Regression testing is conducted by the QA team re-running technical test cases after code changes — not by business users evaluating real workflows with real data. HR employees don't run regression test suites.
explanations.b: Performance testing is conducted by QA/performance engineers measuring system metrics under load — not by business users evaluating workflow suitability. If HR finds the payroll processing takes too long, they might report it as a UAT finding, but the 15 HR employees are not running load generators.
explanations.c: Smoke testing is a 15-minute technical check run by the QA team to confirm basic functionality — not a 2-week business validation exercise with 15 HR employees.
explanations.d: USER ACCEPTANCE TESTING (UAT) is the final testing phase before go-live where ACTUAL END USERS (or their representatives) validate that: the system meets their real BUSINESS REQUIREMENTS; the system supports their actual WORKFLOWS (not just the documented specifications); the USABILITY is acceptable; EDGE CASES that business users know about are handled correctly. UAT characteristics: performed by business users, not QA engineers; uses real (or realistic) data and real business scenarios; results in formal acceptance or rejection; acceptance = authorization to go live; rejection = specific defects/gaps to be corrected before re-testing. UAT is the BUSINESS VALIDATION gate — it answers 'Does this system actually work for us?' rather than 'Does it work technically?'

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Quality & performance management — test plan and testing cycles; quality assurance planning
questions.text: A project manager is planning quality assurance for a 6-month software project. The QA lead recommends developing a test plan before testing begins. Which elements should the test plan include?

answers.text: Only the list of test cases — the test plan is simply a catalog of tests to be executed
Only the defect tracking tool configuration — the test plan specifies which tool will track defects
Only the UAT schedule — earlier testing phases are managed by developers without a formal plan

Testing scope and objectives; test types to be performed (unit, smoke, regression, performance, UAT) and their sequence; test environment requirements; entry and exit criteria for each testing phase; roles and responsibilities; defect management process; and testing schedule aligned with the project timeline

explanations.a: A test plan is a comprehensive governance document, not just a list of tests. The list of test cases is a separate, supporting artifact (test case specifications) — the plan defines how, when, and by whom testing is conducted.
explanations.b: Defect tracking tool configuration is one small component of the test plan, not its entirety. The plan covers strategy, schedule, scope, criteria, and governance.
explanations.c: All testing phases benefit from formal planning — unit test standards, environment setup, entry/exit criteria, and regression test automation all require planning decisions made before testing begins.
explanations.d: A comprehensive TEST PLAN includes: SCOPE: what is in scope for testing (which modules, features, integrations) and what is explicitly out of scope; OBJECTIVES: what the testing must prove (all SLA requirements met, no severity-1 defects remain); TEST TYPES AND SEQUENCE: unit testing → smoke testing → integration testing → regression testing → performance testing → UAT (each phase has defined inputs and outputs); TEST ENVIRONMENT: what environments are needed (development, QA, staging, production-equivalent); hardware/software requirements; data requirements (anonymized production data for UAT); ENTRY CRITERIA: what must be true before each phase begins (e.g., 'unit tests 95% pass rate before integration testing begins'); EXIT CRITERIA: what must be true before each phase is considered complete (e.g., 'zero P1 defects, <3 P2 defects before proceeding to UAT'); ROLES AND RESPONSIBILITIES: who writes test cases? who executes? who approves test results?; DEFECT MANAGEMENT: how are defects categorized (severity/priority), tracked, and resolved?; TESTING SCHEDULE: when does each testing phase begin and end, with dependencies on development milestones.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Quality & performance management — audits and inspections; quality assurance vs. quality control
questions.text: A project manager schedules a formal quality audit of the development process midway through the project. The audit team reviews: whether coding standards are being followed, whether code reviews are being conducted for every merge, whether test coverage targets are being met, and whether defect tracking procedures are being adhered to. What is the PRIMARY purpose of this audit?

answers.text: To identify which developers are writing the most defects so they can be assigned additional training
To verify that quality PROCESSES are being followed correctly (quality assurance) — ensuring the team is using practices likely to produce a quality outcome, not just inspecting the product output
To test the software product for defects — audits are equivalent to quality control testing
To determine whether the project is on schedule — audits review the project timeline and Gantt chart

explanations.a: Identifying which individuals write the most defects is a developer performance management activity, not a quality audit objective. Quality audits assess PROCESSES, not individual performance metrics.
explanations.b: QUALITY AUDIT vs. QUALITY CONTROL: QUALITY AUDIT (Quality Assurance): examines whether quality PROCESSES are being followed. Are we doing the right things the right way? Is the process designed to produce quality outcomes? Examples: Are code reviews being conducted consistently? Are test coverage standards being maintained? Are coding standards being followed? Are defects being tracked and resolved per the defect management process? QUALITY CONTROL: inspects the PRODUCT output for defects. Does the product meet its quality requirements? Examples: defect testing, UAT, performance testing. The audit described is QA — it is evaluating the PROCESS, not the product. The rationale: if the right processes are consistently followed (code reviews, testing standards, coding standards), quality product outcomes are more likely. Process quality is a leading indicator of product quality.
explanations.c: Testing for defects in the software product is Quality Control — it inspects the product output. A process audit does not execute tests or examine the software for functional correctness.
explanations.d: Audits review whether processes are followed, not whether the project is on schedule. Schedule management is handled through status reports, schedule variance analysis, and earned value management — not quality audits.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Quality & performance management — forecasting; EAC; ETC; performance-based projection
questions.text: A project has: Budget at Completion (BAC) = $400,000; Earned Value (EV) = $200,000 (50% complete); Actual Cost (AC) = $240,000; Cost Performance Index (CPI) = EV/AC = 0.833. Using the performance-based Estimate at Completion (EAC = BAC/CPI), what is the projected final cost, and what does this indicate?

answers.text: EAC = $400,000 — the project will finish on budget because 50% is complete
EAC = $480,016 — the EAC is calculated by adding the actual cost to the remaining budget
EAC = $480,193 (approximately $480,000) — BAC/CPI = $400,000/0.833 = $480,193; the project is projected to cost approximately $80,000 more than budgeted if current cost efficiency continues
EAC = $200,000 — the EAC equals the earned value already achieved

explanations.a: The project is NOT on track to finish at $400,000. With a CPI of 0.833 (meaning the team gets $0.833 of value for every $1 spent), continuing at this efficiency will produce a cost overrun. The EAC reflects this reality.
explanations.b: $480,016 is close to the correct answer but the formula used is different (AC + remaining budget adjusted). The standard performance-based EAC formula is BAC/CPI.
explanations.c: FORECASTING with Estimate at Completion (EAC): COST PERFORMANCE INDEX (CPI) = EV / AC = $200,000 / $240,000 = 0.833. CPI < 1.0 means the project is OVER BUDGET (spending more than the work is worth). EAC (performance-based) = BAC / CPI = $400,000 / 0.833 = $480,193. INTERPRETATION: if the project continues at its current cost efficiency (CPI = 0.833), the final total cost will be approximately $480,000 — approximately $80,000 over the original $400,000 budget. This is the most pessimistic but often most realistic EAC formula because it assumes past performance predicts future performance. Actions triggered: the project manager must identify why costs are 20% above earned value; implement corrective actions (reduce scope, improve efficiency, request additional budget authorization); report the projected overrun to the sponsor. Estimate to Complete (ETC) = EAC − AC = $480,000 − $240,000 = $240,000 remaining to spend.
explanations.d: EAC cannot equal EV — EV represents work completed to date, not projected final cost. The EAC must always be at least equal to the AC (you cannot 'unspend' money already spent).

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Quality & performance management — assess methods; KPIs; quality management concepts
questions.text: A project team tracks three quality KPIs over five sprints: Defect Density (defects per 1,000 lines of code), Test Coverage (% of code covered by automated tests), and Escaped Defects (defects found in production after each sprint's release). In Sprint 5, defect density dropped to 0.8 (from 2.1 in Sprint 1), test coverage rose to 87% (from 45% in Sprint 1), but escaped defects increased to 5 (from 2 in Sprint 1). How should the project manager interpret this seemingly contradictory quality data?

answers.text: The quality program is fully successful — defect density and test coverage improvements confirm the team is doing better
The test coverage metric is wrong — 87% coverage should prevent all production defects

The data reveals a QUALITY MEASUREMENT GAP: the team is writing fewer defects (lower density) and testing more code (higher coverage), but the tests are not covering the RIGHT scenarios — the 13% uncovered code paths likely contain the bugs escaping to production; the team should analyze which types of defects are escaping and whether they fall in untested code paths, then prioritize test coverage in those areas
Escaped defects increasing means the project should stop all releases until defect density reaches zero

explanations.a: Escaped defects increasing from 2 to 5 means MORE production defects per sprint — this is a quality REGRESSION in the most customer-impacting metric. Celebrating lower defect density while ignoring worsening escaped defects misreads the quality picture.
explanations.b: 87% test coverage does not prevent all production defects. Coverage measures the percentage of code EXECUTED by tests — not whether the tests verify correct behavior, and not whether the tests cover the right scenarios. A test that executes code but asserts nothing provides coverage but no quality assurance.
explanations.c: QUALITY MEASUREMENT INSIGHT: Three metrics tell a coherent story when interpreted together: DEFECT DENSITY (↓ 2.1 → 0.8): developers are writing cleaner code. Good signal — fewer defects being introduced in the code written. TEST COVERAGE (↑ 45% → 87%): more code is being executed by automated tests. Good signal — testing is more comprehensive. ESCAPED DEFECTS (↑ 2 → 5): more defects are reaching production. Bad signal — the most important quality metric (customer impact) is WORSENING despite the other improvements. INTERPRETATION: the tests are covering more code but may not be covering the RIGHT code paths or business scenarios. Specifically: the 13% uncovered code may contain complex business logic prone to defects; or tests are running code paths but not validating edge cases that cause production failures. ROOT CAUSE INVESTIGATION: audit which types of escaped defects are occurring; map them to code areas and test coverage gaps; prioritize test scenario improvement in high-risk business logic areas. The lesson: test COVERAGE quantity alone is insufficient — test QUALITY (are the right scenarios verified?) matters equally.
explanations.d: Halting all releases until defect density reaches zero is impractical (zero defect density is unrealistic in practice) and misidentifies the problem. The issue is test scenario quality, not development volume.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Quality & performance management — test plan and testing cycles; all 6 test types in correct sequence
questions.text: A project team is preparing a quality assurance plan for a new banking application. They need to sequence their testing cycles correctly. The team has planned: smoke testing, unit testing, performance testing, regression testing, user acceptance testing, and stress testing. Which sequence represents the MOST logical and effective testing order?

answers.text: UAT → Performance → Smoke → Unit → Regression → Stress
Unit → Smoke → Regression → Performance → Stress → UAT
Stress → UAT → Unit → Smoke → Regression → Performance
Performance → Unit → UAT → Smoke → Stress → Regression

explanations.a: Starting with UAT means business users are testing before the technical team has verified that the system even works at a basic level — UAT would be immediately disrupted by defects that earlier testing phases should have caught.
explanations.b: OPTIMAL TESTING SEQUENCE for a banking application: (1) UNIT TESTING: developers test individual functions in isolation first — catches defects at the code level, earliest and cheapest to fix; each module proven individually before integration; (2) SMOKE TESTING: after the build is assembled from tested units, a quick stability check confirms the integrated build is viable enough for full testing; prevents wasting QA time on a fundamentally broken build; (3) REGRESSION TESTING: comprehensive re-execution of all previously passed tests to confirm nothing was broken during the build/integration; verifies the full scope of existing functionality before deeper testing; (4) PERFORMANCE TESTING: validates the system meets SLA performance requirements under expected load; runs after functional correctness is confirmed (no point measuring performance of broken functionality); banking applications have strict SLAs; (5) STRESS TESTING: pushes beyond normal limits to find breaking points; performed after performance baseline is established; understanding failure behavior is critical for a banking system; (6) USER ACCEPTANCE TESTING (UAT): the final gate — actual bank employees validate real business workflows with real scenarios; occurs last because it is the most expensive to fix issues at this stage; requires a fully functional, performance-verified system.
explanations.c: Starting with stress testing before unit testing or smoke testing makes no sense — the system has not been verified at a basic level before being pushed to its breaking point.
explanations.d: Starting with performance testing before unit and smoke testing attempts to measure performance of potentially defect-ridden, unverified code — performance results would be meaningless and the testing would be disrupted by defects.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Quality & performance management — cost and schedule performance; EVM interpretation
questions.text: A project performance report shows: CPI = 1.12 and SPI = 0.87. What does this combination indicate about project health, and what questions should the project manager investigate?

answers.text: CPI = 1.12 means the project is over budget; SPI = 0.87 means the project is ahead of schedule — a mixed result requiring no immediate action

CPI = 1.12 (> 1.0 = under budget — getting more value per dollar spent than planned); SPI = 0.87 (< 1.0 = behind schedule — accomplishing less planned work per period than planned); the project is under budget but behind schedule; the PM should investigate whether the schedule delay is causing the cost efficiency (fewer people spending = lower actual cost) or if there is a genuine efficiency improvement, and whether the schedule delay will become a budget problem if additional effort is needed to recover
Both metrics indicate the project is performing well — any CPI and SPI values above 0.5 are satisfactory
CPI = 1.12 means the project timeline is compressed; SPI = 0.87 means the project is under budget

explanations.a: CPI > 1.0 means UNDER BUDGET (not over budget). SPI < 1.0 means BEHIND SCHEDULE (not ahead of schedule). The directions are reversed in option A.
explanations.b: EARNED VALUE METRICS INTERPRETATION: CPI (Cost Performance Index) = EV / AC: CPI = 1.12 > 1.0 → FAVORABLE — the project is getting $1.12 of value for every $1.00 spent (under budget). SPI (Schedule Performance Index) = EV / PV: SPI = 0.87 < 1.0 → UNFAVORABLE — the project is only accomplishing 87% of the planned work per period (behind schedule). COMBINED INTERPRETATION: Under budget + Behind schedule is a common pattern with a specific warning: the apparent cost efficiency may be ARTIFICIAL — if the team is behind schedule, they may not have spent the money planned for this period yet. When they eventually catch up (or try to), additional resources (overtime, contractors) may erode the apparent cost surplus. INVESTIGATION QUESTIONS: (1) Is the cost efficiency genuine (team is truly more productive) or artificial (team is behind, hasn't yet spent planned resources)? (2) What is causing the schedule delay? (resource constraints? scope clarification? technical complexity?) (3) Can the schedule be recovered within the current budget, or will recovery require additional resources that erode the cost surplus? (4) What is the risk to the critical path — is the SPI delay affecting milestone dates? (5) What is the EAC — does the forecast project final cost remain under budget even after schedule recovery?
explanations.c: CPI and SPI values below 1.0 are unfavorable. An SPI of 0.87 is not 'satisfactory' — it means the project is 13% behind schedule on a performance basis. The '> 0.5 threshold' has no basis in project management standards.
explanations.d: CPI measures cost efficiency, not schedule compression. SPI measures schedule efficiency, not budget. The interpretations in option D are reversed.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Quality & performance management — post-implementation support/warranty period
questions.text: A software project goes live on March 1. The contract includes a 90-day post-implementation support period. On April 15 (45 days post-launch), a significant defect is discovered in the reporting module. On June 15 (106 days post-launch), a second defect is discovered in the payroll module. Under the post-implementation support/warranty period, how should these defects be handled?

answers.text: Both defects are the client's responsibility — once the project team goes live, all defects become operational issues

The April 15 defect (within the 90-day warranty period) is the project team's responsibility to fix at no additional charge; the June 15 defect (after the 90-day warranty) may require a new service agreement or be billable to the client, depending on contract terms
Both defects are the project team's responsibility indefinitely — all defects discovered after go-live must be fixed by the original project team
Neither defect can be fixed — once the project closes, no further changes are permitted to the delivered system

explanations.a: The 90-day post-implementation support period is specifically designed to cover defects discovered after go-live — the project team retains responsibility for these during the warranty period. Transferring all responsibility to the client at go-live would leave unresolved defects without any accountability.
explanations.b: POST-IMPLEMENTATION SUPPORT / WARRANTY PERIOD: most software delivery contracts include a defined period after go-live during which the delivery team is responsible for fixing defects at no additional cost to the client. Purpose: real-world usage reveals defects that testing did not catch; the warranty period acknowledges that no software is perfectly tested; provides the client with risk protection immediately post-launch. APRIL 15 DEFECT (45 days post-launch, within 90-day warranty): the project team is contractually obligated to investigate and fix this defect at no additional charge; the client should report the defect through the agreed defect reporting channel; the team should apply the agreed service level for defect resolution (e.g., P1 defects fixed within 48 hours). JUNE 15 DEFECT (106 days post-launch, outside 90-day warranty): the warranty period has expired; the project team's contractual obligation for no-charge defect fixes has ended; resolution options depend on the contract: (a) a maintenance agreement may have been established to cover post-warranty support; (b) the team can quote a separate remediation engagement; (c) the client's internal IT team handles it.
explanations.c: Indefinite post-launch responsibility is not standard practice and is not contractually defined. The warranty period bounds the project team's obligation. Indefinite responsibility would make software projects economically unsustainable.
explanations.d: Projects can and do have post-go-live support periods during which changes (defect fixes) are made by the original team. Project closure refers to closing the primary project activities, not permanently preventing any future changes to the system.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Quality & performance management — critical path analysis; upcoming milestones; schedule impact on quality
questions.text: A project manager reviews the project schedule and identifies that UAT (currently planned for 15 business days) is on the critical path with no float. A 3-day testing delay in the prior phase is threatening to compress UAT to 12 days. The sponsor suggests 'just running UAT faster.' What risks does this compression create, and what should the project manager recommend?

answers.text: No risks — UAT is equally effective whether conducted in 12 or 15 days

Compressing UAT from 15 to 12 days (20% reduction) creates quality risk: fewer test scenarios can be executed, complex business workflows may not be fully validated, defects may escape to production; the PM should recommend either recovering the lost 3 days earlier in the schedule (overtime/parallel work in prior phase), or formally accepting the compressed UAT risk through a change request documenting the reduced coverage and potential consequences
The sponsor's suggestion should be immediately accepted — sponsor authority means UAT duration decisions are final
Cancel UAT entirely and go live sooner — if 15 days cannot be maintained, UAT provides insufficient value

explanations.a: UAT quality is directly related to the time available for testers to execute test scenarios and discover defects. A 20% reduction in available time means 20% fewer test cycles or rushed execution of all scenarios — both reduce defect detection capability.
explanations.b: CRITICAL PATH AND QUALITY ANALYSIS: UAT on the critical path with no float means any delay to UAT directly delays go-live. The sponsor's desire to maintain the delivery date is understandable, but compressing UAT has quality consequences: (1) QUALITY RISK of 12-day UAT: 20% fewer test scenarios can be executed at normal pace; or all scenarios are rushed — testers have less time to explore edge cases, report detailed observations, or investigate suspicious behavior; complex business workflows (payroll edge cases, exception handling, multi-system integrations) are most likely to be under-tested in compressed UAT; these are also the most costly defects to fix post-launch. (2) PM RECOMMENDATIONS: Option A (Preferred): recover the 3 days earlier in the schedule — authorize overtime in the current testing phase; accelerate the prior phase's remaining work; use parallel testing approaches if possible. Option B (Risk acceptance): if recovery is not possible, formally document the compressed UAT scope, test coverage gaps, and increased production defect risk; the sponsor accepts this risk through a formal change request — go-live decision is made with full knowledge of the quality trade-off. The PM's role: present the risk clearly and objectively; give the sponsor the information to decide; don't simply comply without disclosure.
explanations.c: Sponsor authority does not eliminate the PM's responsibility to identify and communicate risks. Accepting a schedule decision without identifying its quality consequences would be a professional failure. The PM should advise the sponsor of the risks before the decision is finalized.
explanations.d: Canceling UAT entirely would eliminate the last business validation gate before production. Any defects surviving all prior testing phases would go directly to production users — the most expensive and reputation-damaging defect discovery path.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Quality & performance management — upcoming milestones and activity identification; quality gates
questions.text: A project manager identifies the following upcoming milestones: UAT Complete (3 weeks away), Go-Live Readiness Review (2 weeks away), and Production Deployment (6 weeks away). The Go-Live Readiness Review is a formal gate where the sponsor approves or delays deployment. What information should the project manager prepare for the Go-Live Readiness Review?

answers.text: Only the budget status — the sponsor's primary concern is cost

A comprehensive readiness report covering: UAT defect status (open P1/P2 defects, waived defects, test coverage achieved); infrastructure readiness (production environment provisioned and tested); training completion status (end users trained?); go-live rollback plan documented and tested; SLA performance test results; outstanding risks and mitigation status; stakeholder sign-off checklist
Only the deployment plan — the sponsor needs to know how the deployment will be executed
A summary of all issues resolved during the project — historical context is the most important information for a go-live review

explanations.a: Budget is one dimension of go-live readiness but far from the only one. A system that is on budget but has critical open defects, untrained users, and no rollback plan is not ready for go-live.
explanations.b: GO-LIVE READINESS REVIEW preparation requires a multi-dimensional readiness assessment: QUALITY READINESS: UAT completion percentage; list of open defects by severity (P1 = show-stoppers; P2 = significant; P3/P4 = acceptable for go-live with agreed remediation timelines); defects formally waived (business-accepted known issues); test coverage achieved vs. planned. TECHNICAL READINESS: production environment provisioned and validated; performance test results vs. SLA requirements; rollback plan documented, tested, and team-rehearsed; monitoring and alerting configured. OPERATIONAL READINESS: end-user training completion rate; help desk briefed and equipped; support processes documented; post-go-live support team on standby. RISK STATUS: outstanding risks and their current status; go-live specific risks and mitigation plans; escalation path for go-live day issues. STAKEHOLDER STATUS: all required sign-offs obtained (IT, security, compliance, business units). The sponsor needs this complete picture to make an informed go/no-go decision.
explanations.c: The deployment plan is necessary but insufficient. The sponsor cannot decide whether to go live based only on HOW the deployment will happen — they need to know WHETHER the system is ready (quality, training, infrastructure, risk).
explanations.d: Historical issue resolution context is valuable for lessons learned but is not the primary content of a go-live readiness review. The review is forward-looking (are we ready to deploy?) not backward-looking (what problems did we solve?).

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Quality & performance management — retrospective/lessons learned; continuous improvement
questions.text: A Waterfall project is completing its development phase before moving to testing. The project manager schedules a lessons-learned session. A team member says: 'We should do lessons learned at the end, not now — we're not done yet.' How should the project manager respond?

answers.text: Agree with the team member — lessons learned should only happen at project close to capture the complete picture

Disagree — lessons learned should be captured throughout the project at key phase transitions and milestones; capturing them now (end of development) ensures that insights are fresh, can improve the testing phase, and contribute to organizational knowledge even if the project isn't complete
Agree — conducting lessons learned now will discourage the team by focusing on problems during active work
Disagree — but only because it is required by the project contract, not because it provides practical value

explanations.a: End-of-project-only lessons learned has two major weaknesses: (1) memory fades — details from the development phase will be forgotten by project close, especially if months pass between phase end and project completion; (2) actionability — insights about development that are captured only after the project ends cannot improve any remaining phases (testing, deployment) of the current project.
explanations.b: LESSONS LEARNED BEST PRACTICE: lessons learned should be captured CONTINUOUSLY throughout the project, not just at close: AT EACH PHASE GATE/TRANSITION: capture what worked, what didn't, and what to do differently in the next phase — while memories are fresh and insights can be applied to upcoming phases; IN AGILE: the sprint retrospective is a structured, regular lessons-learned session every sprint — the formalized version of continuous improvement; VALUE OF CURRENT LESSONS-LEARNED SESSION: End of development insights can improve the testing phase (e.g., 'we discovered the integration is more complex than anticipated — testing should allocate additional time for integration test cycles'); fresh memories produce better insights than 6-month-old recollections; organizational knowledge base benefits immediately (other projects can apply these insights now). TIMING PRINCIPLE: the best time to capture a lesson is when it is still fresh. Waiting until project close reduces quality, actionability, and organizational value.
explanations.c: Effective lessons-learned sessions are structured to be constructive, not blame-focused. They celebrate successes ('what went well') alongside identifying improvement opportunities. When conducted properly, they improve team morale and engagement — not discourage it.
explanations.d: Lessons learned have genuine practical value: they improve current project phases; they contribute to organizational process improvement; they reduce repetition of mistakes across projects. Framing them as a purely contractual obligation misrepresents their purpose.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Quality & performance management — quality management concepts; verification/validation; audits
questions.text: A project manager wants to establish a comprehensive quality management approach for a healthcare IT project. Which combination of quality activities provides the MOST complete coverage?

answers.text: UAT only — if end users accept the system, all other quality activities are redundant
Automated unit tests only — if all individual functions are correct, the integrated system will be correct

A multi-layered approach: unit testing (code-level correctness); integration testing (component interactions); regression testing (change impact); performance/stress testing (SLA and breaking point validation); quality audits (process adherence); formal verification (specification compliance) and validation (business need confirmation); UAT (business acceptance); post-go-live monitoring and support — each layer catches different defect types that others may miss
Performance testing and UAT only — technical and business validation are the only tests that matter for healthcare systems

explanations.a: UAT catches defects that matter to business users but is inefficient and expensive as the only quality mechanism. Defects found in UAT have already passed through all development phases — they are expensive to fix and may require significant re-work. Earlier testing phases catch defects at lower cost.
explanations.b: Unit tests verify individual functions in isolation.
