The project is in serious trouble: the original critical path is 4 weeks behind; a previously non-critical path has become critical (creating a new critical path or extending the project further); the team's consistent 15% productivity shortfall suggests a systemic problem, not a temporary blip; recovery requires immediate root cause analysis, corrective action on productivity, resource analysis, and a sponsor decision on scope, budget, or timeline
Simply rebaseline — update the schedule to reflect current performance and the project is back on track
Accelerate only the newly critical path — the original critical path can be addressed later

explanations.a: SPI of 0.85 means the team is accomplishing 85% of planned work per period — 15% behind pace. At 3 months into a 12-month project, a 15% productivity shortfall projects to approximately 1.8 months of additional duration (15% of 12 months). Combined with 4 weeks already behind on the critical path and a new critical path emerging, this is a serious schedule problem requiring immediate attention.
explanations.b: COMPREHENSIVE SCHEDULE ASSESSMENT: CRITICAL PATH STATUS: original critical path is 4 weeks behind — these 4 weeks directly extend the project end date unless compressed; EMERGING CRITICAL PATH: a previously non-critical path has consumed its 2-week float and is now critical — the project now has two critical paths (or the original critical path has lengthened by 2 additional weeks if the newly critical path is longer). This means there are now MORE activities that must be on time for the project to finish on schedule; SYSTEMIC PRODUCTIVITY SHORTFALL: 3 consecutive months at 85% velocity is not a random fluctuation — it is a systematic problem requiring root cause analysis. Potential causes: team over-estimated their velocity; work is consistently harder than estimated; team is consistently interrupted/context-switching; resource availability is lower than planned; RECOVERY ANALYSIS for sponsor: OPTION A (Time extension): present the realistic projected end date based on current SPI (15-18 months instead of 12); OPTION B (Crash the critical path): add resources to critical path activities — calculate cost and time savings; OPTION C (Scope reduction): identify features that can be deferred to a Phase 2 release to bring the work within the original timeline; OPTION D (Hybrid): combine modest crashing + targeted scope reduction for a cost-effective recovery. ROOT CAUSE ACTION: regardless of which option is chosen, the 15% productivity shortfall must be investigated and addressed — otherwise, even a compressed or rebaselined schedule will fall behind again.
explanations.c: Simply rebaselining accepts the current poor performance as the new standard without addressing the root cause. If the team continues at 85% velocity after rebaselining, they will be 15% behind the new baseline too.
explanations.d: The original critical path (4 weeks behind) is the primary schedule risk. Focusing only on the newly critical path while ignoring the 4-week delay on the original critical path provides incomplete recovery.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Schedule development — estimating techniques: parametric estimating; historical data
questions.text: A project manager knows from historical data that the organization's development team writes and tests 50 lines of production code per developer-day. The new module requires approximately 2,000 lines of code. The team has 4 developers. Using parametric estimating, what is the estimated duration for the module?

answers.text: 10 days (2,000 lines ÷ 50 lines/developer-day = 40 developer-days ÷ 4 developers = 10 working days)
2,000 days (one day per line of code)
50 days (2,000 lines ÷ 4 developers = 500 lines each, then estimated as 50 days without applying the rate)
400 days (2,000 lines × 50 lines-per-day productivity without accounting for team size)

explanations.a: PARAMETRIC ESTIMATING calculation: Step 1: Total developer-days needed = 2,000 lines ÷ 50 lines/developer-day = 40 developer-days. Step 2: Duration with 4 developers = 40 developer-days ÷ 4 developers = 10 working days. PARAMETRIC ESTIMATING uses a statistical relationship (the parameter — 50 lines/developer-day from historical data) to calculate the estimate. Key characteristics: more accurate than analogous estimating when the parameter relationship is well-established; assumes the historical rate is applicable to the new project's context; can scale with quantity (doubling the code doubles the estimate). Limitations: the 50 lines/developer-day parameter may not account for: code complexity variations; new technology learning curves; integration complexity (lines of code doesn't capture integration effort); rework. The estimate of 10 days represents a starting point that should be refined with additional context.
explanations.b: 1 day per line of code would be an extreme underproductivity assumption. At 50 lines/developer-day from historical data, 2,000 lines represents 40 developer-days — not 2,000 days.
explanations.c: 500 lines per developer (2,000 ÷ 4) is correct partitioning, but then 50 days without applying the 50-lines/developer-day rate is mathematically inconsistent. The calculation should be: 500 lines ÷ 50 lines/developer-day = 10 days per developer = 10 days total duration (since all 4 work simultaneously). 50 days would imply 1 line/developer-day — far below the stated productivity rate.
explanations.d: 2,000 × 50 inverts the formula — this multiplies lines by the productivity rate rather than dividing by it.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Schedule development — story estimation/story points; velocity; sprint cadence; Agile forecasting
questions.text: An Agile team has completed 4 sprints with the following velocities: Sprint 1: 18 points, Sprint 2: 22 points, Sprint 3: 20 points, Sprint 4: 24 points. The product backlog contains 200 story points of remaining work. The client asks: 'When will we be done?' How should the project manager respond?

answers.text: 'We will be done in exactly 200 ÷ 24 = 8.3 sprints' — use the most recent velocity as the forecast
'We cannot forecast — Agile projects have no end dates'

Calculate the average velocity: (18+22+20+24)/4 = 21 story points per sprint; forecast: 200 points ÷ 21 points/sprint ≈ 9.5 sprints; provide a range: if velocity stays around 18-24, the team needs approximately 8-11 sprints; add the sprint duration to convert sprints to calendar time; caveat that the forecast updates every sprint as velocity data grows
'We will be done in 10 sprints' — round up from the average-velocity calculation and add 5% for buffer

explanations.a: Using only the most recent velocity (24 points) may be optimistic — the team's velocity has ranged from 18-24. A single sprint's performance is noisy; a multi-sprint average is more reliable for forecasting.
explanations.b: Agile projects absolutely can and should be forecasted. The difference from Waterfall is that Agile forecasts are probabilistic ranges that update every sprint, not fixed point estimates. 'No end dates in Agile' is a misconception.
explanations.c: AGILE RELEASE FORECASTING using velocity: AVERAGE VELOCITY: (18 + 22 + 20 + 24) / 4 = 84 / 4 = 21 story points per sprint. POINT ESTIMATE: 200 ÷ 21 = 9.52 → approximately 10 sprints. RANGE (acknowledging velocity variability): Optimistic (24 sp/sprint): 200 ÷ 24 = 8.3 sprints → ~9 sprints; Pessimistic (18 sp/sprint): 200 ÷ 18 = 11.1 sprints → ~12 sprints. CALENDAR CONVERSION: if sprints are 2 weeks: 9.5 sprints × 2 weeks = 19 weeks ≈ 5 months. IMPORTANT CAVEATS TO COMMUNICATE: velocity includes completed stories (meeting Definition of Done) — partially completed work does not count; the backlog estimate may change as stories are refined; new stories may be added; velocity typically stabilizes as teams mature (first few sprints are often lower as team learns); forecast updates every sprint — the client gets a new, more accurate forecast every 2 weeks.
explanations.d: '10 sprints' with a 5% buffer applied arbitrarily is less informative than a data-driven range. The approach in C is more rigorous and communicates the uncertainty honestly.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Schedule development — scheduling tools; comparing Waterfall vs. Agile scheduling tools
questions.text: A project manager must choose a scheduling tool for a new IT project. The project uses Scrum methodology with 2-week sprints, cross-functional teams, and requires real-time collaboration across three time zones. Which tool category BEST fits these requirements?

answers.text: A traditional Gantt chart tool (e.g., Microsoft Project) — all projects need Gantt charts for schedule management

An Agile project management tool (e.g., Jira, Azure DevOps, Trello, Linear) — supports sprint planning, backlog management, kanban/task boards, velocity tracking, and real-time collaboration across distributed teams
A spreadsheet (Excel/Google Sheets) — simple tools are always superior for scheduling regardless of project methodology
Paper task boards — physical boards are always more engaging than digital tools for Scrum teams

explanations.a: Microsoft Project is optimized for Waterfall/traditional project management — Gantt charts, critical path, resource loading. While it has some Agile features, it is not designed for sprint planning, product backlog management, or the task-board visualization central to Scrum. It also has limited real-time collaboration features for distributed teams.
explanations.b: AGILE PROJECT MANAGEMENT TOOLS are purpose-built for Scrum and Agile workflows: SPRINT PLANNING: product backlog, sprint backlog, story point estimation, capacity planning; KANBAN/TASK BOARDS: visual work-in-progress tracking (To Do → In Progress → Done) with real-time updates; VELOCITY TRACKING: automatic velocity charts from sprint completion data; BACKLOG MANAGEMENT: hierarchical structure (epics → stories → tasks), prioritization, filtering; REPORTING: burndown charts, sprint reports, team velocity, cumulative flow diagrams; COLLABORATION: real-time updates visible to all team members instantly; notifications; DISTRIBUTED TEAM SUPPORT: cloud-based access from any time zone; comment threads; @mentions for asynchronous coordination. Jira, Azure DevOps, Trello, GitHub Projects, and Linear are leading options with these capabilities.
explanations.c: Spreadsheets can be used for simple scheduling but lack: real-time multi-user collaboration without version conflicts; automated sprint metrics; visual task boards; burndown chart generation; backlog management features. For a cross-timezone Scrum team, spreadsheet scheduling creates more problems than it solves.
explanations.d: Paper task boards require physical co-location. For a team across three time zones, physical boards are inaccessible to the majority of the team — the opposite of the collaboration requirement specified.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Schedule development — schedule compression: crashing; adding resources to critical path
questions.text: A project is 3 weeks behind schedule on its critical path. The sponsor insists the go-live date cannot move. The project manager analyzes crashing (adding resources) as an option. Activity X on the critical path currently takes 6 weeks with 2 developers ($8,000/week each). Adding 2 more developers would compress it to 4 weeks ($8,000 × 4 developers = $32,000/week). What is the cost of crashing this activity and when is crashing appropriate?

answers.text: Crashing cost = $0 — adding developers doesn't cost more if they're already on payroll

Crashing cost for Activity X: additional 2 weeks saved; current cost: 2 devs × $8K × 6 weeks = $96K; crashed cost: 4 devs × $8K × 4 weeks = $128K; crashing cost = $128K − $96K = $32K additional cost to save 2 weeks; crashing is appropriate when the cost of delay exceeds the crashing cost
Crashing cost = $32K per week (add 2 developers at $8K each); crash only the most expensive activities to maximize cost efficiency
Crashing is never appropriate — schedule compression always reduces quality

explanations.a: Additional developers cost money — whether from overtime pay, contractor fees, or opportunity cost of pulling resources from other projects. Crashing always has a direct or indirect cost.
explanations.b: CRASHING COST ANALYSIS: CURRENT (2 developers, 6 weeks): cost = 2 × $8,000 × 6 = $96,000. CRASHED (4 developers, 4 weeks): cost = 4 × $8,000 × 4 = $128,000. CRASHING COST = $128,000 − $96,000 = $32,000 additional cost to save 2 weeks. CRASH COST PER WEEK SAVED = $32,000 / 2 weeks = $16,000 per week. WHEN IS CRASHING APPROPRIATE: if the cost of a 2-week schedule delay exceeds $32,000 (contract penalties, lost revenue, additional overhead), crashing is economically justified. CRASHING PRINCIPLE: crash ONLY activities on the critical path (non-critical activities don't affect the end date); crash the activity with the LOWEST COST per week of compression first (best schedule compression ROI); crashing has diminishing returns — at some point, adding more people reduces efficiency (too many people on one task creates coordination overhead and Brooks's Law effects); crashing always costs more than the original schedule — the project manager must have authorization for the additional budget.
explanations.c: 'Crash only the most expensive activities' is backwards — crash the CHEAPEST activities per week saved first (best ROI) to minimize the additional cost for maximum schedule compression.
explanations.d: Crashing adds resources, not scope changes that reduce quality. Quality risks in crashing come from: onboarding time for new team members; coordination overhead; ramp-up time. Managed properly, crashing can compress the schedule without quality reduction.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Schedule development — integrating critical path, float, dependency types, compression, and Agile concepts
questions.text: A hybrid project (waterfall governance + Agile execution) has the following situation: the critical path runs through a vendor-dependency (external dependency — vendor must provide API access before integration can begin), an integration sprint (hard logic — cannot integrate before API access), and UAT. The project is 4 weeks behind because the vendor is delayed. The sponsor asks the project manager to 'make up the 4 weeks.' Analyze the options and constraints.

answers.text: Fast-track the vendor dependency — begin integration work before the API is available to save 4 weeks

The vendor dependency is an EXTERNAL and HARD LOGIC dependency — it cannot be fast-tracked or crashed; recovery options are limited: (1) negotiate with the vendor to expedite delivery (escalate, offer incentives, explore SLA enforcement); (2) use mock APIs/sandbox environments to prepare integration work in parallel while waiting for real access; (3) evaluate whether UAT can be accelerated or parallelized (if it has discretionary dependencies); (4) escalate to sponsor: 4 weeks cannot be 'made up' without either vendor acceleration, additional resources for UAT compression, or accepting a later end date — present these options with realistic cost/timeline analysis
Add 10 more developers to the integration sprint — crashing always recovers schedule on any dependency type
Remove UAT from the scope — eliminating the last phase recovers 4 weeks without affecting the vendor dependency

explanations.a: Fast-tracking is only possible for SOFT LOGIC (discretionary) dependencies. Integrating before API access is physically impossible — there is nothing to integrate against. The dependency is hard logic, making fast-tracking impossible.
explanations.b: HYBRID PROJECT SCHEDULE RECOVERY ANALYSIS with external hard-logic dependency: CONSTRAINT IDENTIFICATION: Vendor API dependency = EXTERNAL + HARD LOGIC. External: the vendor's timeline is outside the project's control. Hard logic: integration cannot begin without API access — this is not a preference, it is a technical requirement. IMPLICATIONS: Fast-tracking is impossible (hard logic). Crashing the dependency is impossible (external — cannot add our resources to the vendor's work). RECOVERY OPTIONS: (1) VENDOR ACCELERATION: escalate within the vendor's organization; invoke SLA provisions or contract penalty clauses for delay; explore whether paying a premium can expedite the vendor's API preparation — this is 'crashing' at the vendor level; (2) PARALLEL PREPARATION WORK: develop integration code against MOCK APIs (simulated, documented) or SANDBOX environments provided by the vendor; when real API access is received, minimal rework is needed → reduces actual integration-after-access time; (3) UAT ACCELERATION: if UAT has discretionary dependencies or excess duration, explore: parallel UAT tracks (different user groups testing simultaneously); UAT preparation work (test scripts, test data, environments) completed before UAT begins; UAT duration reduction via risk-acceptance of reduced coverage; (4) HONEST SPONSOR COMMUNICATION: the 4-week delay was caused by an external event outside project control; partial recovery may be possible through options 1-3; the sponsor needs realistic expectations — options with trade-offs (cost, quality, timeline).
explanations.c: Adding developers helps activities where resources are the constraint. The vendor dependency is not a resourcing problem on the project team's side — additional developers cannot access or deliver the vendor's API. Crashing only works for internal, resource-constrained activities.
explanations.d: Removing UAT eliminates a critical quality gate that validates the entire system against business requirements. For a system with external vendor integration (additional complexity and uncertainty), removing UAT would be high-risk and potentially unacceptable to the client.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Schedule development — tasks; epics; stories; Definition of Done; sprint execution
questions.text: During sprint execution, the Scrum team's task board shows the story 'As a customer, I can reset my password via email' as 'Done.' However, the QA engineer points out that while the email trigger code is written and the password update function works in isolation, the end-to-end flow has not been tested, the feature is not deployed to the staging environment, and no code review has been completed. Is the story 'Done'?

answers.text: Yes — the core coding work is complete; the other items are optional extra steps
Yes — once the developer marks it as Done in the task board, it is Done by definition

No — the story is NOT done; the Definition of Done (DoD) for this team requires code review, end-to-end testing, and staging deployment before a story can be marked Done; marking incomplete work as Done reduces team credibility, creates technical debt, and produces inaccurate velocity data
Yes — QA testing and code review can be done in the next sprint without affecting the current sprint's Done status

explanations.a: Code implementation is one task within a story — it is not the complete story. The Definition of Done defines the complete set of criteria a story must meet before it counts as delivered increment.
explanations.b: The task board reflects what the team has declared Done, not what actually is Done. Inaccurate task board marking is a Scrum process discipline problem, not a definition question.
explanations.c: DEFINITION OF DONE (DoD): the DoD is a shared team agreement on the minimum quality criteria that must be met before a story (or sprint increment) is considered complete. A typical software development team's DoD might include: code implementation complete; code review passed; unit tests written and passing; end-to-end feature testing passing; deployed to staging environment; documentation updated; acceptance criteria verified. The story 'reset password via email' is NOT Done because: end-to-end flow not tested → may fail in ways isolated tests didn't catch; not deployed to staging → may have environment-specific issues; code review not complete → potential code quality or security issues. CONSEQUENCES of false 'Done': velocity inflation (sprints appear to complete more than they actually deliver); technical debt accumulation (incomplete items become 'definition debt' that slows future sprints); stakeholder trust erosion (sprint review demonstrates work that isn't actually finished); production risk (unreviewed, untested code deployed to production).
explanations.d: Testing and code review done in the next sprint means the story was NEVER 'Done' in the sprint it was claimed — and the next sprint is now spending capacity on work from the previous sprint. This pattern produces consistently incomplete sprints and inflated velocity.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Schedule development — float/slack; critical path; near-critical paths; schedule risk
questions.text: A project has a critical path of 30 days. Path 2 has 25 days total duration (5 days of float). Path 3 has 27 days total duration (3 days of float). The project manager is monitoring schedule risk. Which path should receive ALMOST as much attention as the critical path and why?

answers.text: Path 2 (5 days float) — largest float means highest schedule risk

Path 3 (3 days float) — nearest-critical path; only 3 days of float before it becomes critical; small delays will consume float and turn Path 3 into a second critical path, extending the project end date
Both paths need equal attention as the critical path — all schedule paths are equally important
Neither path needs attention — only the critical path matters until float is completely consumed

explanations.a: Counterintuitively, LARGER float means LOWER immediate risk. Path 2 with 5 days of float has more buffer before it becomes critical. Path 3 with only 3 days of float is more vulnerable to becoming critical.
explanations.b: NEAR-CRITICAL PATH MONITORING: paths with very little float are 'near-critical' — they warrant heightened monitoring because small delays can turn them into critical paths. Path 3 (3 days float) is a near-critical path: only a 3-day delay in ANY activity on Path 3 will consume all float and make Path 3 critical; if Path 3 becomes critical AND the original critical path extends, the project may have TWO critical paths simultaneously — increasing schedule complexity and risk; any further delays on Path 3 directly extend the project end date. PATH 2 (5 days float): significant buffer — would need a 5-day delay before becoming critical; warrants routine monitoring but less intensive attention than Path 3. NEAR-CRITICAL PATH MANAGEMENT PRINCIPLE: paths with float approaching zero should be treated almost as carefully as the critical path; delays that seem non-critical can quickly become critical as float erodes.
explanations.c: Not all schedule paths are equally important — that is precisely why critical path analysis and float calculation exist. Float quantifies the relative risk of each path.
explanations.d: Waiting until float is completely consumed means the non-critical path is already critical — reactive management at that point can no longer prevent the impact. Proactive monitoring of near-critical paths is essential to avoid surprises.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Schedule development — comprehensive: all schedule management dimensions integrated
questions.text: A project manager inherits a 6-month project at the 2-month mark. She discovers: the schedule baseline was created with no contingency reserves; all dependencies were assumed to be FS without analyzing whether any can run in parallel; the team's velocity data shows consistently 20% lower output than estimated; the critical path has no float; and three major external vendor dependencies are untracked. What are the MOST urgent schedule management corrections needed?

answers.text: Accept all problems and continue — inherited projects should not be changed from their original plan
Immediately rebaseline with 50% longer duration — add 50% to every estimate to compensate for all problems simultaneously

Prioritize corrections: (1) IMMEDIATE — identify and track all 3 external vendor dependencies (untracked external risks); (2) THIS WEEK — re-analyze dependency types (identify which FS dependencies can be parallelized to compress schedule); (3) THIS WEEK — add appropriate contingency reserves to high-risk activities; (4) THIS MONTH — conduct root cause analysis on the 20% velocity shortfall and implement corrective actions; (5) THIS MONTH — develop a realistic completion forecast based on actual velocity and present options to the sponsor
Focus only on the velocity shortfall — fixing team productivity will automatically resolve all other schedule problems

explanations.a: Inheriting a project with serious schedule management deficiencies and doing nothing creates known risks that will materialize without intervention. The project manager's professional obligation is to correct identified problems within their authority and escalate those requiring authorization.
explanations.b: Adding 50% to all estimates without analysis creates an unjustifiably pessimistic schedule that may unnecessarily alarm stakeholders and waste budget. Corrections should be targeted and evidence-based.
explanations.c: PRIORITIZED SCHEDULE MANAGEMENT CORRECTIONS: PRIORITY 1 — IMMEDIATE: External vendor dependencies (untracked): untracked external dependencies are blind spots. If a vendor fails to deliver and it's not being monitored, the project team has no warning. IMMEDIATE ACTION: catalog all three vendor dependencies; identify what each vendor must provide and by when; establish weekly vendor status check-ins; assess each as a risk in the risk register; develop contingency plans for vendor delay. PRIORITY 2 — THIS WEEK: Dependency re-analysis: the assumption that all dependencies are FS may be unnecessarily constraining the schedule. Many FS relationships are actually soft logic that can be fast-tracked. REVIEW: for each FS dependency, ask 'could these activities run in parallel?' — soft logic can be parallelized to compress the schedule; identify specific fast-tracking opportunities on the critical path. Contingency reserves: the schedule has no buffer for risk. Without reserves, every risk event that materializes creates immediate baseline pressure. ADD: targeted contingency buffers to high-risk activities (based on qualitative risk assessment). PRIORITY 3 — THIS MONTH: Velocity root cause: 20% shortfall over 2 months is systemic — it requires investigation (estimation methodology? interruptions? scope clarity? resource availability?). CORRECT: implement targeted improvements based on root cause; adjust future sprint commitments to reflect actual velocity. Realistic forecast: develop a completion forecast based on actual velocity (not original estimates); present sponsor with: current projected completion date; options (scope reduction, resource addition, timeline extension). This systematic approach addresses the most dangerous issues first (unmonitored external risks) while building toward a fully corrected schedule management approach.
explanations.d: Team velocity is one of four identified problems. External vendor dependencies, dependency type errors, and missing contingency reserves are independent problems that will cause schedule failures regardless of whether the velocity shortfall is corrected.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Meeting management — meeting type: stand-up (daily standup); purpose and structure
questions.text: A Scrum team holds a 15-minute meeting every morning where each team member answers three questions: What did I complete yesterday? What will I work on today? Are there any blockers preventing my progress? This meeting is BEST described as:

answers.text: A daily stand-up (daily Scrum) — a short synchronization meeting for the development team to inspect progress toward the sprint goal and plan the next 24 hours
A status meeting — the project manager collects weekly progress reports from all team members
A steering committee meeting — executives review the team's progress and provide strategic guidance
A retrospective — the team reflects on what went well and what to improve

explanations.a: DAILY STAND-UP (Daily Scrum): a timeboxed (15 minutes maximum), synchronous meeting held every working day; the three questions provide structure: YESTERDAY: ensures accountability and progress visibility; TODAY: creates a shared plan for the team; BLOCKERS: surfaces impediments early so the Scrum master can help remove them. Key characteristics: standing up reduces time waste; held at the same time and place each day; for the development team (not a reporting meeting for management); the Scrum master facilitates and removes identified blockers; the product owner may observe; the purpose is TEAM SYNCHRONIZATION, not status reporting to a superior.
explanations.b: Status meetings are typically longer, less frequent (weekly or biweekly), and involve reporting to management. The three-question structure described is the daily Scrum format, not a management status report.
explanations.c: A steering committee meeting involves senior executives and governance-level decisions — not 15-minute daily stand-ups with the development team answering three questions.
explanations.d: A retrospective examines how the team works and identifies process improvements — it occurs at the end of each sprint, not daily, and is much broader in scope than the three-question structure described.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Meeting management — meeting type: status meeting; purpose and frequency
questions.text: A project manager holds a weekly 45-minute meeting where team leads report on the progress of their work streams, budget actuals, upcoming milestones, and open risks and issues. This is BEST described as:

answers.text: A brainstorming session — the team is generating new ideas for the project
A project steering committee meeting — executives are overseeing the project's strategic direction
A workshop — team members are collaboratively solving a complex problem
A project status meeting — a regular, structured meeting to review progress, surface issues, and align the team on current project health across all dimensions

explanations.a: Brainstorming sessions focus on GENERATING ideas, options, or solutions — not reporting progress, budget actuals, or risks. A brainstorming meeting is creative and generative, not analytical.
explanations.b: Steering committee meetings involve executives (sponsor, senior leadership) at a governance level, typically less frequently (monthly or quarterly) with higher-level information. This weekly meeting with team leads is an operational status meeting.
explanations.c: A workshop is an intensive, focused working session to solve a specific problem, design a solution, or create a specific output — not a regular reporting meeting.
explanations.d: PROJECT STATUS MEETING: a regular, recurring meeting to maintain shared visibility across the project team: FREQUENCY: weekly is common for active projects; biweekly for less active phases; ATTENDEES: project manager + team leads or work stream owners; CONTENT: progress against schedule milestones; budget vs. actual costs; risk and issue status updates; upcoming milestone readiness; decisions needed. The status meeting enables the PM to: identify variances early; coordinate across work streams; escalate issues to the appropriate authority; ensure the team has a consistent picture of project health. Unlike the steering committee, the status meeting is operational (internal team), not governance (executive oversight).

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Meeting management — agenda setting/publishing; meeting preparation
questions.text: Why should a project meeting agenda be published to all attendees BEFORE the meeting begins?

answers.text: To give attendees time to prepare relevant information, formulate questions, and arrive ready to contribute — maximizing meeting effectiveness and respecting participants' time
To allow attendees to decide whether they want to attend based on the topics listed
To satisfy a regulatory requirement that all project meetings be documented in advance
To allow the project manager to cancel the meeting if the agenda items are resolved before the meeting time

explanations.a: PRE-MEETING AGENDA DISTRIBUTION: publishing the agenda 24-48 hours before the meeting: ENABLES PREPARATION: attendees can review relevant documents, pull data, or prepare presentations before arriving; IMPROVES MEETING QUALITY: participants arrive with their thinking done — the meeting is for discussion, decisions, and alignment, not for first-time information delivery; RESPECTS TIME: attendees who need to prepare specific items can budget preparation time; SETS EXPECTATIONS: everyone knows what the meeting is for and what outcomes are expected; IMPROVES OUTCOMES: agenda-less or late-agenda meetings frequently run long, go off-topic, and produce no decisions — well-prepared meetings are 40-60% more productive; AGENDA ELEMENTS: topic list with time allocations; objective for each agenda item (inform, discuss, decide); pre-read materials noted; presenter/facilitator for each item; desired outcome for the overall meeting.
explanations.b: While attendees may learn from the agenda that their presence is optional for certain topics, the primary purpose of pre-publishing is meeting preparation, not optional attendance management. Making attendance decisions based on the agenda is a secondary benefit.
explanations.c: There is no universal regulatory requirement for pre-meeting agenda publication. It is a best practice, not a compliance obligation.
explanations.d: Canceling a meeting because agenda items are resolved is a legitimate use case — but it is a secondary benefit of having an agenda, not its primary purpose.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Meeting management — timeboxing; meeting efficiency
questions.text: A project manager assigns 10 minutes for each agenda item in a 60-minute meeting and appoints a timekeeper to signal when each item's time expires. Items not fully resolved are parked for follow-up. This practice is BEST described as:

answers.text: Timeboxing — assigning a fixed maximum time to each agenda item or meeting event to prevent overruns and keep the meeting focused and on schedule
Meeting cancellation — limiting time on items effectively cancels discussion
Meeting minutes — documenting what was discussed in each time slot
Scope creep — adding new topics to the agenda during the meeting

explanations.a: TIMEBOXING: a time management technique that assigns a fixed, maximum time allocation to a specific activity or agenda item. In meeting management: AGENDA TIMEBOXING: 'Risk review: 10 minutes; Budget update: 8 minutes; Blocker resolution: 12 minutes'; prevents any single topic from consuming the entire meeting; SPRINT TIMEBOXING: all Scrum events are timeboxed (daily standup: 15 min; sprint planning: up to 2 hrs/sprint week; sprint review: up to 4 hrs/sprint; retrospective: up to 3 hrs/sprint); PARKING LOT: items that run over their timebox are 'parked' (noted for follow-up offline or in a future meeting) — this ensures the meeting ends on time while acknowledging that not everything resolved in the room; BENEFITS: respects all attendees' time; prevents dominant speakers from monopolizing discussion; creates predictability; forces prioritization of discussion time.
explanations.b: Timeboxing does not cancel discussion — it bounds it. The purpose is to ensure every topic receives some attention within the allocated time, not to prevent discussion altogether.
explanations.c: Meeting minutes document what was DISCUSSED and DECIDED — they are a record of the meeting, not a time management technique.
explanations.d: Scope creep in meetings refers to unplanned topics being added during the meeting — not the time allocation practice of timeboxing.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Meeting management — action items; follow-ups; accountability
questions.text: At the end of a project meeting, the scribe documents several action items. What information should be captured for EACH action item to ensure accountability and follow-through?

answers.text: Description of the action, the single person responsible (owner), and the target completion date — providing clear accountability for each commitment
Only the description of the task — the team will self-organize to complete it
A list of everyone who attended the meeting — all attendees share responsibility for all action items
The action item rank by priority — only the highest-priority item needs to be tracked

explanations.a: EFFECTIVE ACTION ITEM DOCUMENTATION requires three elements: DESCRIPTION: what specifically needs to be done? (specific enough to be actionable — not 'investigate the risk' but 'contact vendor ABC for delivery commitment letter by Friday'); OWNER: a single named person responsible for completing or driving the action. Multiple owners = no accountability (diffusion of responsibility); DUE DATE: a specific target completion date. Without a date, 'soon' becomes 'never.' These three elements create a complete commitment: 'Maria will obtain vendor commitment letter by March 10.' At the next meeting, Maria's status is reviewed. This structure enables: accountability (Maria knows she is responsible); follow-up (the next meeting starts with a review of open action items); escalation (if Maria cannot complete it, early warning allows intervention).
explanations.b: Without an owner and a due date, an action item is simply a statement of intent with no accountability mechanism. Most undated, unowned action items are never completed.
explanations.c: 'Everyone is responsible' = no one is responsible. The diffusion of responsibility principle confirms that assigning tasks to a group without a single owner produces far lower completion rates than single-owner assignments.
explanations.d: All action items must be tracked — not just the highest priority. Lower-priority actions that are never tracked become forgotten commitments that surface as problems later.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Meeting management — facilitator role; scribe role; meeting roles
questions.text: In a project meeting, what are the DISTINCT responsibilities of the FACILITATOR and the SCRIBE?

answers.text: Facilitator: guides the meeting process — keeps the discussion on topic, manages participation, ensures time is respected, drives toward decisions; Scribe: documents the meeting — records key discussion points, decisions made, and action items in real time
Both roles are identical — the facilitator and scribe do the same job with different titles
Facilitator: takes attendance and distributes materials; Scribe: presents the agenda and runs the meeting
The facilitator and scribe are both optional — project meetings do not require designated roles

explanations.a: MEETING ROLE DISTINCTIONS: FACILITATOR: focuses on the PROCESS of the meeting — how the meeting runs; manages agenda items and time (timeboxing); balances participation (drawing out quiet voices, managing dominant speakers); keeps discussion on track (redirects off-topic conversations to parking lot); guides the group toward decisions without dictating them; manages conflict if discussions become heated; asks probing questions to deepen discussion; does NOT focus on content documentation. SCRIBE (note-taker): focuses on the CONTENT of the meeting — what was said and decided; records key discussion points, decisions, and rationale in real time; captures all action items (owner, description, due date); publishes meeting minutes after the meeting; does NOT manage the meeting process. COMBINED BENEFIT: separating these roles improves both: the facilitator focuses entirely on guiding; the scribe focuses entirely on documentation — producing better meeting dynamics AND better records.
explanations.b: The facilitator and scribe have fundamentally different responsibilities — combining them creates a problem: a person simultaneously trying to guide discussion AND document it will do both tasks poorly. Splitting the roles allows each person to focus.
explanations.c: Distributing materials is an administrative pre-meeting task (can be done by anyone). The facilitator RUNS the meeting process; the scribe DOCUMENTS it — not the other way around.
explanations.d: Designated roles significantly improve meeting effectiveness. Meetings without facilitation tend to go off-topic, over time, and without clear decisions. Meetings without a scribe produce no record of what was decided.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Meeting management — meeting type: brainstorming; facilitation rules
questions.text: A project team needs to identify all possible risks for a new product launch. The project manager decides to hold a brainstorming session. Which facilitation approach BEST maximizes the effectiveness of the brainstorming meeting?

answers.text: Defer judgment during idea generation: all ideas are recorded without criticism or evaluation; the team generates as many risks as possible in a defined timebox; evaluation and prioritization happen AFTER the generation phase is complete
Have the most senior team member propose risks first, then invite others to add to the list — seniority ensures the most important risks are captured first
Allow team members to argue against risks in real time — critical discussion during generation produces better quality risks
Limit brainstorming to 5 minutes — shorter sessions produce more creative ideas due to time pressure

explanations.a: EFFECTIVE BRAINSTORMING facilitation principles: DEFER JUDGMENT (golden rule): all ideas are recorded as stated — no criticism, dismissal, or debate during generation; when people fear their ideas will be immediately criticized, they self-censor; deferred judgment produces 30-50% more ideas than evaluated brainstorming; QUANTITY OVER QUALITY: generate as many risks as possible — quantity creates a more comprehensive risk register; EQUAL PARTICIPATION: round-robin or timed contributions ensure every voice is heard, preventing dominant personalities from controlling the list; VISUAL DISPLAY: use a whiteboard or shared screen to display all generated risks — seeing them sparks new connections; TIMEBOX GENERATION: define a fixed generation period (e.g., 20 minutes); then move to EVALUATION: after generation is complete, the group evaluates, combines, and prioritizes the list; duplicate ideas are merged; implausible risks may be removed after discussion. This two-phase approach (generate → evaluate) consistently outperforms single-phase evaluated brainstorming.
explanations.b: Starting with the most senior person creates anchoring bias — team members unconsciously limit their own suggestions to variations of what the senior person proposed. Junior members may also self-censor concerns that seem to contradict the senior person's list.
explanations.c: Real-time criticism during idea generation is the most common brainstorming mistake. It: inhibits creative thinking; silences participants who fear judgment; produces fewer, lower-quality ideas. Criticism belongs in the evaluation phase, not the generation phase.
explanations.d: Five minutes is too short for thorough risk identification on a product launch — risk brainstorming typically benefits from 20-45 minutes of structured generation. Time pressure beyond a reasonable limit reduces quality, not increases it.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Meeting management — meeting type: workshop; focus group; differences and use cases
questions.text: A project team needs to gather stakeholder requirements for a new HR system. Two meeting options are proposed: Option A — a half-day session where a cross-functional group of HR managers, IT staff, and payroll specialists collaboratively map current processes, identify pain points, and design future-state workflows together. Option B — a 1-hour session where 8 representative HR end users are asked open-ended questions about their daily challenges with the current system while an observer takes notes. Which meeting types are these and when is each most appropriate?

answers.text: Option A: workshop (intensive collaborative working session producing a specific deliverable — future-state workflow designs); Option B: focus group (facilitated discussion with representative users to gather qualitative input on experiences and preferences)
Both are workshops — all collaborative requirements meetings are workshops
Option A: focus group; Option B: workshop — the difference is only in the number of attendees
Both are status meetings — requirements gathering is a status reporting activity

explanations.a: WORKSHOP vs. FOCUS GROUP: WORKSHOP (Option A): PURPOSE: intense, collaborative work session where cross-functional participants build, design, or solve something together; CHARACTERISTICS: typically half-day to multi-day; requires cross-functional participant mix (HR + IT + payroll); produces a specific tangible OUTPUT (workflow diagrams, requirements documents, process designs); highly interactive and work-focused; FACILITATOR's role is to guide the collaborative work process; BEST FOR: complex requirement elicitation requiring multiple perspectives; process design; solution architecture; problem-solving requiring diverse expertise. FOCUS GROUP (Option B): PURPOSE: gather qualitative information about user experiences, opinions, preferences, or perceptions; CHARACTERISTICS: 6-12 representative participants; facilitator guides DISCUSSION (not construction); observer documents responses; no specific work product is produced — the output is INFORMATION (what users think/feel/need); questions are open-ended and exploratory; BEST FOR: understanding user experience with current systems; validating feature concepts before building; gathering qualitative requirements insight. The two meetings serve different requirements gathering purposes and produce different outputs.
explanations.b: A focus group is specifically designed to gather qualitative user input through facilitated discussion — not to collaboratively produce workflow designs. The distinction matters because workshops produce outputs; focus groups gather information.
explanations.c: The number of attendees is not the distinguishing factor — a workshop can have 5 people; a focus group can have 10. The distinction is about WHAT THEY DO (build together vs. discuss and share) and what they PRODUCE (deliverable vs. information).
explanations.d: Status meetings report on current project progress — they are not requirements gathering activities.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Meeting management — meeting type: JAD (Joint Application Development) / JAR (Joint Application Review) session
questions.text: A software project team holds a structured session where business users and IT developers work together for 3 days to jointly design the application's data model, user interface flows, and business rules — producing a detailed requirements specification that all parties sign off on. This meeting type is BEST described as:

answers.text: A daily stand-up — short synchronization meetings between business and IT
A steering committee meeting — executives are aligning business and IT strategy
A brainstorming session — the team is generating ideas for the new application

A Joint Application Development (JAD) session — a structured, facilitated meeting bringing business users and IT developers together to jointly design system requirements, eliminating the traditional iterative back-and-forth of separate requirements gathering and review cycles

explanations.a: Daily stand-ups are 15-minute synchronization meetings for development teams — not multi-day collaborative design sessions with business and IT.
explanations.b: Steering committee meetings involve executives at a governance level — not developers and business users jointly designing data models and UI flows.
explanations.c: Brainstorming sessions are creative idea generation meetings. JAD sessions are structured, facilitated working sessions with specific deliverable outputs — the opposite of open-ended brainstorming.
explanations.d: JAD (Joint Application Development) session: ORIGIN: developed by IBM in the 1970s as an alternative to the lengthy, disconnected requirements gathering process; PURPOSE: bring business users and IT developers together in a structured, facilitated session to jointly define system requirements — eliminating communication gaps; CHARACTERISTICS: typically multi-day (2-5 days); structured facilitation by a neutral JAD facilitator; participants include business SMEs, end users, IT architects, and developers; produces signed-off, joint requirements documentation; BENEFITS: reduces requirements misunderstanding (business and IT develop a shared language); compresses the requirements phase significantly; produces requirements that both parties understand and commit to; CONTRAST WITH TRADITIONAL: traditional requirements gathering = analysts interview users separately → write requirements → IT reviews → business reviews → negotiate → revise → (iterate multiple times). JAD = all parties together → joint design → single sign-off. JAR (Joint Application Review) applies the same collaborative approach to reviewing and validating existing requirements or designs.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Meeting management — meeting type: project steering committee meeting; executive governance
questions.text: A project manager prepares for a quarterly steering committee meeting attended by the CEO, CFO, CIO, and the project's executive sponsor. The project is on schedule but has an emerging risk requiring a $200,000 budget increase decision. What should the project manager prepare and how should the meeting be structured?

answers.text: Provide detailed sprint-by-sprint technical status — executives need the full technical context to make governance decisions
Send a detailed technical report and cancel the meeting — executives can read the report without meeting
Hold the meeting as an informal discussion without a formal agenda — steering committees prefer unstructured conversation

Present an executive-level summary: overall project status (RAG indicator), top 3 risks, budget vs. actuals, next milestone date, the budget increase request with business case and options, and a recommendation — governance meetings focus on high-level decisions, not operational detail

explanations.a: CEO, CFO, and CIO do not need sprint-by-sprint technical status in a governance meeting. Detailed technical content overwhelms executives, obscures the decision-needed signal, and wastes governance meeting time. The project manager's role is to translate operational detail into governance-relevant summary.
explanations.b: A written report without a meeting cannot capture the real-time discussion, clarifying questions, and interactive decision-making process that a steering committee meeting is designed to provide. The budget decision requires committee discussion and formal authorization.
explanations.c: Steering committees require formal, structured agendas. These senior executives have limited time — unstructured meetings fail to reach decisions, waste time, and frustrate participants.
explanations.d: STEERING COMMITTEE MEETING PREPARATION: EXECUTIVE AUDIENCE: these are senior decision-makers with limited time and a broad portfolio of responsibilities. Communications must be: concise (1-2 page pre-read max); visual (dashboard-style, RAG indicators); decision-oriented (clear what the committee needs to approve or decide). MEETING STRUCTURE: Opening (5 min): overall project status summary (Green/Amber/Red + narrative); Financial status (5 min): budget vs. actual, forecast to completion; Risk summary (5 min): top 3 risks, status, mitigation; Next milestone (2 min): what is coming up and readiness; KEY AGENDA ITEM — Budget decision (15 min): background on the emerging risk; three options (proceed as planned/accept risk, increase budget by $200K/mitigate, defer scope to reduce cost); PM recommendation with rationale; committee decides; Wrap-up (3 min): action items from the committee. A formal agenda is always required for steering committees — unstructured conversation wastes executive time and rarely produces decisions.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Meeting management — meeting type: refinement (backlog refinement/grooming); Agile
questions.text: An Agile team holds a weekly meeting where the product owner and development team review upcoming user stories, clarify acceptance criteria, break large stories into smaller ones, and re-estimate story points as more information becomes available. This meeting is BEST described as:

answers.text: Sprint planning — the team is selecting stories for the next sprint
A status meeting — the team is reporting progress on current sprint work
Sprint retrospective — the team is reflecting on what to improve in their process
Backlog refinement (grooming) — the team reviews, clarifies, estimates, and prepares backlog items to ensure they are 'ready' for upcoming sprint planning sessions

explanations.a: Sprint planning SELECTS stories from the refined backlog for the upcoming sprint and creates the sprint plan. Refinement PREPARES the backlog items before they reach sprint planning — it is the prerequisite step that makes sprint planning efficient.
explanations.b: Status meetings report on current progress — refinement is a forward-looking preparation activity for future sprints.
explanations.c: The sprint retrospective focuses on PROCESS improvements (how the team works) — not on preparing the product backlog.
explanations.d: BACKLOG REFINEMENT (Grooming): PURPOSE: keep the product backlog healthy — ensuring upcoming items are well-understood, properly sized, and ready for sprint planning; ACTIVITIES: CLARIFICATION: product owner explains the intent and context of upcoming stories; developers ask questions to understand what 'done' looks like; ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA REVIEW: each story's acceptance criteria are reviewed and refined — what must be true for this story to be accepted?; STORY SPLITTING: large stories (epics or oversized stories) that won't fit in a sprint are broken into smaller, sprint-sized stories; ESTIMATION: story point estimates are updated as more information becomes available — initial rough estimates get refined; DEPENDENCY IDENTIFICATION: dependencies between stories are surfaced; FREQUENCY: typically weekly or bi-weekly, consuming 5-10% of sprint capacity; BENEFIT: refined backlogs make sprint planning faster (stories are already understood) and more accurate (stories are properly sized). Without regular refinement, sprint planning becomes the inefficient place where story clarity and estimation happen — slowing the team and producing unreliable sprint commitments.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Meeting management — meeting type: task-setting meeting; work assignment and planning
questions.text: A project manager holds a meeting at the start of a new project phase where team members receive their specific work assignments, deliverable responsibilities, and deadlines for the upcoming month. Team members also have the opportunity to ask questions and raise concerns about their assignments. This meeting is BEST described as:

answers.text: A retrospective — the team reflects on the previous phase before beginning the new one
A brainstorming session — the team generates ideas for how to complete the assignments
A focus group — end users provide input on the task assignments
A task-setting meeting — work is formally assigned to team members with clear deliverables, deadlines, and the opportunity to clarify expectations before work begins

explanations.a: A retrospective is a process reflection meeting — it focuses on HOW the team worked, not on assigning new work. A retrospective is backward-looking; a task-setting meeting is forward-looking.
explanations.b: Brainstorming is creative idea generation. The meeting described involves specific assignment of pre-defined work, not generating new ideas.
explanations.c: Focus groups gather qualitative input from representative users about their experiences or preferences — not a mechanism for assigning project work to team members.
explanations.d: TASK-SETTING MEETING: a structured assignment meeting that transitions the team from planning into execution: ASSIGNMENTS: specific deliverables and work packages are assigned to named team members; DEADLINES: target completion dates for each assignment are communicated; EXPECTATIONS: clarity on quality standards, format requirements, and success criteria for each deliverable; Q&A OPPORTUNITY: team members can ask clarifying questions before work begins — catching misunderstandings early when they are cheapest to correct; COMMITMENT: team members acknowledge their assignments and flag capacity or dependency concerns. TIMING: at phase transitions, sprint starts (Agile sprint planning is effectively a task-setting meeting), or when new work is introduced. VALUE: reduces the chance that team members begin work based on different assumptions about scope, quality, or timeline.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Meeting management — meeting minutes; documentation; follow-up
questions.text: A project team holds a critical decision-making meeting. The project manager distributes meeting minutes 5 days later. Several attendees respond saying the minutes don't accurately reflect the decisions made. This situation could have been prevented by:

answers.text: Not taking meeting minutes at all — documentation creates more problems than it solves

Distributing the minutes within 24 hours while memories are fresh; having the scribe read back key decisions and action items at the end of the meeting for real-time confirmation; and requesting a review window where attendees can submit corrections within 48 hours
Making the meeting shorter — shorter meetings produce less ambiguity in minutes
Distributing minutes only to the project manager and sponsor — limited distribution reduces the risk of disputes

explanations.a: Meeting minutes are essential governance documentation — they capture decisions made, action items assigned, and issues discussed. The solution to inaccurate minutes is better minutes practices, not eliminating minutes.
explanations.b: MEETING MINUTES BEST PRACTICES: TIMELINESS: distribute within 24 hours (48 at most) while memories are fresh. After 5 days, attendees' memories have faded and reconstructed — making discrepancies more likely; END-OF-MEETING VERBAL CONFIRMATION: the scribe or facilitator reads back the key decisions and action items at the end of the meeting: 'Before we close — let me confirm what we decided. Decision 1: We will use Vendor A for cloud hosting. Action item: Sarah will send Vendor A the contract by March 5. Does anyone see anything I missed or captured incorrectly?' — this real-time verification catches errors while everyone is present; REVIEW WINDOW: send the draft minutes with a 24-48 hour review window for corrections; this provides a structured, time-bounded correction mechanism; CLEAR DECISION NOTATION: clearly label decisions made vs. items discussed (not decided); DISTRIBUTION LIST: all attendees plus any stakeholders who need the record.
explanations.c: Meeting length does not determine minutes accuracy — a 15-minute meeting with poor minutes practice can produce disputes; a 3-hour meeting with good practice can produce clear, accepted minutes.
explanations.d: Distributing minutes only to senior leaders defeats the governance purpose — all participants need the meeting record to know their action items, understand the decisions made, and act on the meeting's outcomes.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Meeting management — meeting type: demonstration/presentation; stakeholder engagement
questions.text: An Agile project team invites the project sponsor and key business stakeholders to watch a live demo of the completed sprint features — showing actual working software in a test environment. The stakeholders provide feedback on what they see and the product owner adjusts the backlog accordingly. Which meeting type is this and what is its PRIMARY purpose?

answers.text: A task-setting meeting — the product owner is assigning new tasks to the development team based on stakeholder feedback
A sprint review / demonstration — showing working software to stakeholders to inspect the increment, gather feedback, and adapt the product backlog based on real observations of the delivered value
A steering committee meeting — executives are making governance decisions about the project
A daily stand-up — a short synchronization event where the team reports progress

explanations.a: Task assignment is a sprint planning or task-setting activity. The meeting described is about showing completed work and gathering feedback, not assigning new work.
explanations.b: SPRINT REVIEW / DEMONSTRATION: the Scrum sprint review is a working software demonstration: PARTICIPANTS: Scrum team + project sponsor + business stakeholders + product owner; WHAT HAPPENS: developers demonstrate working features in a test/staging environment; stakeholders interact with the software (not a PowerPoint slideshow — actual working software); product owner accepts or rejects completed items based on acceptance criteria; stakeholders provide feedback on features, priorities, and product direction; product backlog is updated based on the feedback; PURPOSE: INSPECT the increment (what was built this sprint?); ADAPT the product backlog (what should be built next based on what we've learned?); MAINTAIN ALIGNMENT: keep stakeholders continuously engaged with actual progress; gather real feedback while changes are still relatively cheap; build trust through demonstrated, measurable progress. This is the Agile mechanism for CONTINUOUS VALIDATION — stakeholders don't wait until final delivery to see if the product meets their needs.
explanations.c: Steering committees focus on governance and strategic decisions — not on live software demonstrations and backlog adaptation.
explanations.d: Daily stand-ups are 15-minute synchronization meetings for the development team — not stakeholder demonstrations lasting 30-90 minutes.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Meeting management — follow-ups; action item tracking; meeting effectiveness
questions.text: A project manager holds a weekly status meeting where action items are identified every week. At the following week's meeting, the project manager discovers that 60% of action items from the previous meeting were not completed. What is the ROOT CAUSE and what corrective action should the project manager take?

answers.text: The team is unprofessional — replace team members who don't complete action items
Hold action item follow-up meetings separately from status meetings — two meetings are better than one
Stop tracking action items — if the team cannot complete them, formal tracking is counterproductive

Diagnose the root cause: are action items unclear? unrealistic? untracked between meetings? owners not held accountable? Then implement: review open action items at the START of every status meeting (not at the end); ensure each action item has a clear owner, specific description, and realistic due date; follow up on overdue items between meetings (not just weekly); investigate whether action items are competing with other priorities

explanations.a: A 60% incomplete rate is a systemic process problem, not an individual character problem. Replacing individuals without fixing the underlying action item management process will produce the same results with new people.
explanations.b: Adding a separate follow-up meeting is overhead that creates more calendar friction without addressing the root cause. The issue is the quality and management of action items, not the number of meetings.
explanations.c: Eliminating action item tracking removes the accountability mechanism entirely. The problem is the quality of tracking and follow-through, not the practice of tracking.
explanations.d: ROOT CAUSE ANALYSIS for action item non-completion: POSSIBLE ROOT CAUSES: UNCLEAR ACTIONS: 'Follow up on the vendor issue' is not actionable; 'Contact vendor PM by Thursday and request delivery date confirmation' is; UNREALISTIC DEADLINES: action items assigned with 1-week deadlines when the work requires 3 weeks; UNTRACKED BETWEEN MEETINGS: nothing reminds owners of their commitments between weekly meetings; NO ACCOUNTABILITY REVIEW: action items from last week are never reviewed at the start of this week's meeting — owners know there's no follow-up; COMPETING PRIORITIES: action items aren't sufficiently urgent relative to other demands; CORRECTIONS: (1) START each status meeting with: 'Let's review last week's action items — [owner], what's the status of [item]?' — this creates visible accountability; (2) IMPROVE DOCUMENTATION: specific, unambiguous description; named owner; specific due date; (3) BETWEEN-MEETING FOLLOW-UP: send a reminder email 2 days before due dates; the project manager or assistant tracks and nudges; (4) ROOT CAUSE INVESTIGATION: if a specific owner consistently misses — is it clarity? Workload? Competing priorities? Address individually.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Meeting management — attendees/target audience; right people in the right meetings
questions.text: A project manager invites 25 people to a 2-hour technical architecture review meeting. Only 6 people (the architecture team) actively contribute; the other 19 observe and contribute nothing. After the meeting, several attendees complain they wasted 2 hours. What meeting management principle was violated and how should future meetings be designed?

answers.text: No principle was violated — large meetings demonstrate project importance and organizational engagement

The RIGHT PEOPLE principle was violated: meetings should include only those who actively contribute or are essential decision-makers; the 19 observers should be replaced with a post-meeting distribution of the meeting minutes, key decisions, and action items
The timeboxing principle was violated — the meeting should have been limited to 30 minutes regardless of the agenda
The scribe principle was violated — with 25 people, a dedicated scribe is required

explanations.a: Twenty-five people spending 2 hours in a meeting where 19 contribute nothing = 38 person-hours wasted. This is a significant organizational cost and a failure of meeting management discipline.
explanations.b: RIGHT PEOPLE IN MEETINGS: ACTIVE PARTICIPANT PRINCIPLE: meetings should include only those who actively contribute (present, discuss, decide) or who must be present for a specific critical reason. For a technical architecture review: SHOULD ATTEND: architecture team members; architect-level reviewers; product owner (to confirm architectural decisions meet business needs); any SMEs contributing technical expertise. SHOULD NOT ATTEND (receive minutes instead): senior executives wanting awareness (they get the summary); team members curious about the architecture (they read the documentation); stakeholders needing to know decisions (they receive meeting minutes). EFFECTIVE APPROACH: small, focused meeting with the right contributors → publish detailed minutes with decisions and action items → send to all interested parties as a RACI notification. This respects everyone's time while ensuring broad awareness of outcomes. The 19 'observers' didn't need to be in the room — they needed the OUTCOME.
explanations.c: Timeboxing manages time within a meeting — it doesn't address the attendee selection problem. A 30-minute meeting with 25 people where 19 contribute nothing is still a waste.
explanations.d: A scribe is valuable for any size meeting — but the primary problem here is inappropriate attendee selection, not the absence of a scribe.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Meeting management — agenda setting; timeboxing; facilitation; meeting effectiveness
questions.text: A project team's weekly status meeting consistently runs 30 minutes over its 1-hour time limit. Investigation reveals: the agenda is sent 10 minutes before the meeting; discussions frequently go off-topic; one team lead dominates discussion; no timekeeper is assigned; and the meeting ends without clear action items. Which COMBINATION of interventions would MOST effectively address these problems?

answers.text: Cancel all meetings — the root cause is that meetings are unnecessary
Extend the meeting to 2 hours — providing more time solves the overrun
Record the meeting and send the recording instead of attending — asynchronous recordings replace live meetings

Publish the agenda 24 hours before with timeboxes for each item; assign a dedicated timekeeper and facilitator; implement a parking lot for off-topic discussions; use round-robin participation to prevent one voice from dominating; end every meeting with action item capture and verbal confirmation before adjourning

explanations.a: The meetings serve a coordination function — the problem is the meeting quality, not the meetings themselves. Canceling removes the coordination mechanism.
explanations.b: Extending the meeting to 2 hours rewards bad meeting habits with more time. The problem is not insufficient time — it is inefficient use of the time available.
explanations.c: Recording replaces the synchronous interaction that makes status meetings valuable (real-time Q&A, collaborative problem-solving, immediate decision-making). Recordings are useful supplements but cannot fully replace live synchronous coordination meetings.
explanations.d: TARGETED INTERVENTIONS matching root causes: ROOT CAUSE 1: agenda sent 10 minutes before → INTERVENTION: publish agenda 24 hours in advance with explicit time allocations per topic; ROOT CAUSE 2: off-topic discussions → INTERVENTION: parking lot (whiteboard or shared doc where off-topic items are noted for separate follow-up); facilitator actively redirects off-topic discussions; ROOT CAUSE 3: one team lead dominates → INTERVENTION: round-robin format where each person is explicitly asked to contribute; facilitator limits individual speaking time; ROOT CAUSE 4: no timekeeper → INTERVENTION: assign a dedicated timekeeper (separate from facilitator); timekeeper signals when each agenda item's time is ending (2-minute warning); ROOT CAUSE 5: no action items captured → INTERVENTION: the final 5 minutes of every meeting are reserved for action item capture; scribe reads back all action items for verbal confirmation before adjourning. These five interventions directly address each of the five identified root causes — producing a meeting that ends on time with clear commitments.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Meeting management — selecting the right meeting type for the situation
questions.text: A project manager has five situations requiring a meeting. Match each situation to the MOST appropriate meeting type: (1) The project team needs to identify all possible failure modes for a new payment system; (2) Business users and IT must design the data model together for a customer database; (3) The CEO and CFO need to approve a $2M budget extension request; (4) End users should share their frustrations with the current invoicing system before requirements are written; (5) The Scrum team reviews their last sprint and commits to process improvements.

answers.text: (1) Focus group; (2) Status meeting; (3) Daily stand-up; (4) Workshop; (5) Sprint planning
(1) Brainstorming; (2) JAD session; (3) Steering committee meeting; (4) Focus group; (5) Sprint retrospective
(1) Steering committee; (2) Brainstorming; (3) Focus group; (4) JAD session; (5) Daily stand-up
(1) Status meeting; (2) Refinement; (3) Sprint review; (4) Task-setting; (5) Workshop

explanations.a: Focus groups gather qualitative user input — not the right format for technical failure mode identification. A status meeting is not how systems are jointly designed. Daily stand-ups are 15 minutes of team synchronization — not budget approval meetings. Workshops produce working artifacts; they don't gather qualitative user frustrations about existing systems. Sprint planning selects work for sprints; it doesn't reflect on process improvements.
explanations.b: MEETING TYPE MATCHING: (1) FAILURE MODE IDENTIFICATION → BRAINSTORMING: the team needs to generate as many failure modes as possible without self-censoring; brainstorming's 'defer judgment' principle produces comprehensive lists; the PM then facilitates prioritization of the generated risks; (2) JOINT DATA MODEL DESIGN → JAD SESSION: Joint Application Development is specifically designed for business users and IT to collaboratively design system components; the structured facilitation produces a jointly owned output; (3) CEO/CFO BUDGET APPROVAL → STEERING COMMITTEE MEETING: executive governance decisions (major budget changes) are the exact purpose of steering committee meetings; the PM presents the business case and the committee decides; (4) USER FRUSTRATIONS WITH CURRENT SYSTEM → FOCUS GROUP: gathering qualitative input from representative users about their experiences with an existing system is the textbook focus group use case; open-ended facilitated discussion produces insights that structured interviews might miss; (5) SCRUM TEAM PROCESS REVIEW → SPRINT RETROSPECTIVE: the retrospective is designed specifically for the Scrum team to inspect how they work (process) and identify improvements — exactly what situation 5 describes.
explanations.c: This option assigns meeting types to situations they clearly don't match — steering committees don't identify technical failure modes; brainstorming doesn't produce data model designs (JAD does); focus groups don't approve budgets.
explanations.d: Status meetings report progress; they don't identify failure modes. Refinement prepares backlog items; it doesn't design systems collaboratively. Sprint reviews demonstrate software; they don't govern budget approvals. Task-setting assigns work; it doesn't gather user frustrations.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Meeting management — facilitator role; managing meeting dynamics
questions.text: During a requirements workshop, two senior stakeholders begin arguing about the priority of two competing feature areas. Their debate consumes 20 minutes with no resolution, and other attendees disengage. As the facilitator, what is the MOST appropriate intervention?

answers.text: Let the debate continue — the most important decisions emerge from unresolved conflict
Take sides with the stakeholder who has higher organizational seniority — senior authority resolves disputes

Intervene to redirect: acknowledge both perspectives as valid; note the disagreement as an unresolved decision for the product owner or sponsor to resolve offline; move the discussion to the parking lot; and continue with the next agenda topic — the facilitator does not decide priority disputes, but ensures the meeting continues productively
End the meeting immediately — stakeholder conflicts make productive workshops impossible

explanations.a: A 20-minute unresolved debate that disengages all other attendees is consuming workshop time and producing no decisions. Letting it continue indefinitely is not facilitation — it is abdicating the facilitator role.
explanations.b: Taking sides violates the facilitator's neutrality principle. A facilitator guides the PROCESS; they do not advocate for positions or impose outcomes. Taking the senior stakeholder's side also risks alienating the other stakeholder and producing a superficial 'resolution' that doesn't reflect genuine consensus.
explanations.c: FACILITATOR INTERVENTION for stakeholder conflict: ACKNOWLEDGE: 'I can see both of you have strong, well-reasoned positions on this. These are both legitimate priorities.' — this validates both perspectives without judging; REFRAME: 'This is exactly the type of priority decision that needs the right decision-making process — not a workshop debate with time pressure.'; PARK IT: 'I'm going to note this as an open priority decision for [product owner/sponsor] to resolve after the workshop, with both your positions documented.'; MOVE ON: 'Can we continue with the next agenda item while we still have everyone together?' The facilitator's role is to: keep the meeting productive; ensure the time of all attendees is used effectively; surface conflicts (not suppress them) but move resolution to the appropriate person/process. Priority disputes between senior stakeholders are not workshop-level decisions — they require the appropriate governance authority (product owner for Agile; sponsor or steering committee for Waterfall).
explanations.d: Ending the meeting over a conflict wastes the investment of all other attendees and the meeting's planning. One conflict point should be parked, not used as a reason to abandon the entire meeting.

questions.name: Project Management Concepts
questions.keyword: Meeting management — agenda setting; meeting structure; inform vs. discuss vs. decide
questions.text: A project manager is designing the agenda for a 90-minute project status meeting. The agenda includes: (A) Q3 milestone status update (5 min, information only); (B) Risk register review and escalation decision for Risk #7 (20 min, decision required); (C) Vendor negotiation strategy discussion (30 min, discuss options); (D) Action item review from last meeting (10 min); (E) Budget vs. actual review (15 min, information only); (F) Open Q&A (10 min). The project manager wants to ensure the MOST IMPORTANT items receive the best attention. How should the agenda be ordered?

answers.text: A, B, C, D, E, F — alphabetical order ensures consistency
F, E, D, C, B, A — reverse order ensures all items are covered

D (action item review), B (decision — Risk #7 escalation), C (strategic discussion — vendor negotiation), A (milestone update), E (budget update), F (open Q&A) — decisions and strategic discussions should be placed early when attention is highest; information items and Q&A toward the end
Open Q&A first — allow open discussion before structured agenda items to warm up the group

explanations.a: Alphabetical agenda ordering has no relationship to meeting effectiveness. The order of agenda items significantly affects what receives the best attention and decision quality.
explanations.b: Reverse order places information items first and decisions last — by the time the decision items arrive, the meeting may be running short on time and attendees' attention has faded.
